Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 50, verse 1:

Surat Qaf, also called Surat al-Basiqat.

It is Meccan, as the majority have stated absolutely. In al-Tahrir (by Ibn 'Ashur? [no]) it is related from Ibn 'Abbas and Qatadah that it is Meccan except for His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And We have certainly created the heavens and the earth﴾ (the verse), which is Medinan, revealed concerning the Jews. Its number of verses is forty-five, by consensus. When, glorified is He, at the end of the preceding surah, He indicated that the faith of those Bedouins was not true faith, and this implies the denial of prophethood and the denial of resurrection, He opened this surah, mighty and majestic is He, with what relates to that. The Prophet (ﷺ) used to recite it often in the Fajr prayer, as in the hadith of Muslim and others from Jabir ibn Samurah, and in the narration of Ibn Majah and others from Qutbah ibn Malik, that he (peace and blessings be upon him) used to recite it in the first rak'ah of the Fajr prayer. Ahmad, Muslim, Abu Dawud, Ibn Majah, al-Tirmidhi and al-Nasa'i related from Abu Waqid al-Laythi that "he (ﷺ) used to recite in the Eid with Qaf and Iqtarabat."

Abu Dawud, al-Bayhaqi, Ibn Majah and Ibn Abi Shaybah related from Umm Hisham bint Harithah, who said: "I did not learn Qaf, wal-Qur'an al-Majid except from the mouth of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ); he used to recite it every Friday on the minbar when he addressed the people."

In the hadith of Ibn Mardawayh from Abu al-'Ala (may Allah be pleased with him), raised to the Prophet: "Learn Qaf, wal-Qur'an al-Majid."

All of this indicates that it is among the greatest of the surahs.

(In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful.) ﴿Qaf. By the glorious Qur'an﴾ — possessing majesty and nobility, in the manner of attributive relation (nisbah), like laabin and tamir (having milk and having dates). Otherwise, the well-known usage is describing the noble Essence by it. The practice of some of them clearly favours this view. It has been objected that this is not known in the form fa'il, as Ibn Hisham said regarding ﴿Indeed, the mercy of Allah is near﴾. But you know that whoever memorises it is a proof against one who does not memorise, and its nobility in this respect compared to other books is clear for non-divine books; as for divine ones, it is due to its inimitability, its not being abrogated by anything else, and its containing, together with its concision, secrets in which each one of them is too narrow. Al-Raghib said: al-majd is breadth in generosity, and its origin is "majadat al-ibil" when the camels fell into a wide, abundant pasture. Describing the Qur'an with it is because of the abundance of noble qualities, worldly and otherwise, that it contains. It may also be that its description with it is because it is the speech of the Majestic (al-Majid), so it is a description by the attribute of its speaker, and the attribution is metaphorical, as in "the Wise Qur'an." Or because whoever knows its meanings and acts by what is in it is glorious (majid) before Allah and before people; so the speech is with an omitted modifier, the pronoun of the modifier being dropped and replaced by its referent. Or fa'il is here in the sense of mufil, like badi' in the sense of mubdi' (originator); but there is discussion regarding the coming of fa'il as an attributive from the form af'ala, and most lexicographers and grammarians have not affirmed it. Most of what was mentioned under His saying, ﴿Sad. By the Qur'an, possessor of the Reminder﴾, applies here, to the point that it has been said: it is possible that Qaf is an imperative from the verbal form fa'ala (to follow), from qafa athrahu, i.e. he followed it, and the meaning is: follow the Qur'an and act by what is in it; but this has not been heard as transmitted. Similar to this is what has been said: that it is an imperative in the sense of qif, i.e. stop at what has been legislated for you and do not transgress it.

Ibn Jarir and Ibn al-Mundhir related from Ibn 'Abbas, who said: Allah created, beyond this earth, a sea encompassing it, and beyond that a mountain called Qaf; the lowest heaven rests upon it. Then beyond that mountain He created an earth like this earth seven times over; then beyond that a sea encompassing it; then beyond that He created a mountain called Qaf, upon which the second heaven rests; until he counted seven earths, seven seas and seven mountains. Then he said: that is His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And the sea, after it, is extended by seven seas﴾.

Ibn Abi al-Dunya in al-'Uqubat and Abu al-Shaykh related from him also that he said: Allah created a mountain called Qaf encompassing the world, whose roots extend to the rock upon which the earth rests. When Allah wishes to shake a town, He commands that mountain, and it moves the vein that lies beneath that town, so it shakes and quakes it; hence one town is shaken and not another.

Ibn al-Mundhir, Abu al-Shaykh in al-'Azamah, al-Hakim and Ibn Mardawayh related from 'Abd Allah ibn Buraydah that he said concerning the verse: Qaf is a mountain of emerald encompassing the world, upon which the sides of the sky rest. 'Abd al-Razzaq related from Mujahid that he also said: it is a mountain encompassing the earth.

Al-Qarafi held that the mountain of Qaf has no existence, and he argued for it with what he argued, then said: "It is not permissible to believe what has no evidence." Ibn Hajar al-Haytami criticised him, saying: "That is refuted by what came from Ibn 'Abbas through chains compiled by the memorisers and a group of those who committed themselves to compiling the sound; and the statement of a Companion of this kind, which has no room for opinion, has the ruling of what is raised to the Prophet (ﷺ): that beyond our earth there is an encompassing sea, then a mountain called Qaf," to the end of what was mentioned earlier. Then he said: "Just as his saying 'it has no existence' is refuted by this, his saying 'it is not permissible to believe, etc.' is refuted too, for if by evidence he means any indication, then these are evidences; or if he means definitive indication, then this is something in which conjecture suffices, as is clear." The end of his words. But what I incline to is what al-Qarafi held, that this mountain has no existence by the testimony of the senses, for they have traversed this earth, land and sea, along the path of the Tropic (of Cancer) many times and did not witness that. To impugn the soundness of these reports, even though some of their transmitters are among those who committed themselves to compiling the sound, is easier than rejecting what the senses testify. This is not a case of denying existence for lack of finding, as is not hidden from those of insight. The matter of earthquakes does not depend on that mountain; rather they arise from vapours, and their seeking to exit together with the firmness of the earth. To deny this is obstinacy for one who has the least share of fairness. And Allah knows best.

It has been differed regarding the answer to the oath. It has been said: it is omitted, indicated by the speech, as if it were said: "By the glorious Qur'an, We have sent it down that you may warn people by it." Abu Hayyan estimated it as: "Indeed you came to them as a warner of the resurrection," and similar to what has been said: "Indeed you are a warner." It has also been said: "They did not reject your command with any proof."

Al-Akhfash, al-Mubarrad and al-Zajjaj said: its estimate is "you will certainly be resurrected." It has been said: it is mentioned explicitly. According to al-Akhfash: ﴿We know what the earth diminishes of them﴾, the lam having been dropped due to the length of the speech. Also from him, and from Ibn Kaysan: ﴿what word he utters﴾. It has been said: ﴿Indeed in that is a reminder﴾, and this is the choice of Muhammad ibn 'Ali al-Tirmidhi. It has been said: ﴿The word is not changed with Me﴾. And from the grammarians of Kufa, it is His saying, exalted is He:

﴿Rather, they wonder that a warner from among themselves has come to them.﴾ What was mentioned first is the one relied upon. "Bal" (rather) here marks an *idrab* (a shift away from a preceding statement) from what the answer to the omitted oath implies. It is as if it were said: "We sent it down so that you might warn people by it, but they did not believe in it. Rather, they made each of the warner and what he warns of an object of arrogance and wonder, even though both are most fitting to what reason requires and most conducive to being received with acceptance." It has also been said that the sense is: "You came to them as a warner about the Resurrection, but they did not accept it. Rather, they wondered, or doubted it." "Rather, they wondered" means that they did not content themselves with doubt and rejection but affirmed the opposite, to the point of regarding it as one of the strange matters. It has also been said that this is an *idrab* from what is understood from describing the Qur'an as "the Glorious." It is as if it were said: "The reason for their refusal to believe in the Qur'an is not that it lacks glory, but their ignorance." By the words of the Exalted, ﴿Rather, they wondered﴾, he alerted to this, because wondering at a thing implies ignorance of its cause.

Al-Kashf said: "This is a good interpretation." (*wa-an jā'ahum*) is with the implied "li-an jā'ahum" (because there came to them). The meaning of (*minhum*) "from among them" is "of their kind," that is, of the human race, or of the Arabs. The plural pronoun in the verse refers to the disbelievers. It has been said that it refers to people in general, but this is not correct.

The words of the Exalted, ﴿So the disbelievers said, "This is a strange thing."﴾ explain their wonder and clarify that it accompanies the utmost denial, with added detail regarding the object of their wonder. "This" points to his being a warner by the Qur'an, peace and blessings be upon him. Their being referred to by a pronoun first serves to indicate that they are identified by what is attributed to them, and their being named explicitly afterwards serves to record their disbelief in its consequence. Alternatively, it is a conjunction of their wonder at the Resurrection with their wonder at the sending of the Messenger. The conjunction with *fa* (then) is because it follows it and branches from it, for when the one sent is denied, what he was sent with is denied too. Moreover, "this" refers to something vague, namely the Resurrection, which is explained by the following denial clause. The context also indicates this, since it shows that there is a warner about it, and it is known that the warning of the prophets, peace be upon them, is primarily about the Resurrection and what follows it.

Placing the explicit noun in place of the pronoun is either because they had already been described by what makes them disbelievers, or to indicate that their wonder at the Resurrection, since it implies their considering God's power too weak for it, is despite their witnessing His power over what is harder than it by the measure of reason, in His wondrous creations. This makes it more reprehensible than the first and more deeply rooted in being disbelief.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 50, verse 3:

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿When we die and become dust—that is a far return?﴾ is an affirmation of wonder and an emphasis of denial, or an explanation of the point of their wonder. The governing element of "idha" (when) is a hidden verb, which needs no explanation because of its extreme fame, and because what follows indicates it. The meaning is: "When we die and become dust, shall we return?" as the warner and the one warned of speak of it, together with the complete contrast between us and life at that time.

His saying, Glorified is He: ﴿That﴾ is a pointer to the point of dispute, which is the return and the resurrection after death. The meaning is: that return ﴿is a far return﴾, that is, far from imagination, or from custom, or from possibility. It has also been said: "al-raj'" (return) means "the thing returned," that is, the answer. One says, "This is the return of your message," meaning its reply. On this view the pointer refers to "When we die..." and so on, and the sentence is part of the speech of God, Exalted. The meaning is: "That is a distant answer from them to their warner." The governing element of "idha" in this case is what the warner indicates of the thing warned of, namely the resurrection; that is, "When we die and become dust, He will resurrect us." It may be said that once it is established that this is their answer to their warner, it is known that he warned them of the resurrection so that this could be a fitting answer to it. Thus it is also an indication of the implied element. So the claim that, if "al-raj'" means "the thing returned," which is the answer, there is no indication in the sentence of the governing element of "idha," is refuted. Indeed, this view is itself far-fetched; rather, Abu Hayyan said: it is a strange notion which the understanding of the Arabs shrinks from grasping.

Al-A'raj, Shayba, Abu Ja'far, Ibn Thabbab, al-A'mash and Ibn Utba, from Ibn 'Amir, read (إذا) with a single hamza in the form of a statement. This may be an interrogative with the hamza of interrogation omitted, and it may be a declarative. In al-Bahr it is said: the response to "idha" is hidden, that is, "When we die and become dust, we will return." Sahib al-Lawami permitted that the response is "that is a far return," on the assumption that the particle of response (fa') is omitted. Some of them permitted this for the response of a conditional in general when it is a nominal sentence, while our companions restricted it to poetry in cases of necessity.

﴿We know what the earth diminishes of them﴾, that is, what the earth consumes of their flesh, bones and hair. This is a rejection of their disbelief in resurrection, by removing what is essentially the basis of it, namely that their parts have scattered, so that they cannot be known until they are restored, according to their corrupt assumption. It was also said: "what the earth diminishes of them" refers to the one who dies and is buried in the earth from among them. The reason for the expression "what" is clear, but the first interpretation is more apparent, and it is what is related from Ibn 'Abbas and Qatada. His words, exalted is He, ﴿And with Us is a Book that preserves﴾, are a generalisation of His knowledge, exalted is He. That is: with Us is a Book that preserves the details of all things, and their deeds are included in it, or it is protected from alteration. The meaning is either to illustrate His knowledge of universals and particulars by the knowledge of one who has a preserving book, from which everything is received, or it is an affirmation of His knowledge, exalted is He, of their being fixed in the Preserved Tablet (al-Lawh al-Mahfuz, the Preserved Tablet) with Him, glorified is He.

That said, the verse contains an allusion to the rejection of a doubt held by those who regard the restoration of the non-existent (i'adat al-ma'dum) as impossible, and thus deny resurrection on this basis, on the premise that the parts of the dead cease to exist rather than merely scattering. Its summary is that when a thing is annihilated and its existence does not continue into the second moment, and then it is recreated in the third moment, it entails an absurd arbitrary judgement to rule that this later existent is in its very self the earlier existent, and not another existent like it that is newly begun. For when it has lost the identity of the first existent, nothing of it remains, of the substance or of the personal accidents, so that the second existent would include it and thereby justify the said judgement, and the arbitrariness would be avoided.

The summary of the rejection is that God, exalted is He, is knowing of the details of all things; He knows their universals and their particulars in the most perfect and complete manner. Thus the non-existent has a particular form (surah juz'iyya) with Him, glorified is He, and so it is preserved with its personal accidents in His eminent knowledge, in a way that distinguishes it from the newly begun existent. Hence arbitrariness does not follow. This is analogous to the preservation of the unity of the imaginal form (al-surah al-khayaliyya) within us after the perceived object has disappeared from the senses: when we see a person and he goes out of our sight, then we see him again, we judge that this person is the one we saw before. This judgement corresponds to reality, and is based upon the certain preservation of the unity of the imaginal form, and none denies this except an obstinate one.

Some of the Ash'ariyya (Ash'arites, the school of al-Ash'ari) said: the non-existent has a particular form that comes about through the attachment of the attribute of sight from the One who brings things into being, who is God, exalted is He. That form does not belong to the newly begun existent, for its form, although it too is a real particular, has not been produced by the attachment of the attribute of sight. There is no doubt that what is produced by the attachment of the attribute of sight is more perfect than what is not so produced, so a clear distinction exists between the two forms. If the unity of the external existent is preserved for us by particular imaginal forms, then its preservation by the particular form that exists for Him, exalted is He, through the attachment of the attribute of sight, is all the more so. End of quotation. This is good, but the verse does not allude to it.

Likewise, it does not hold according to those who deny that God, glorified is He, sees non-existent things absolutely. However, those people hold that the identities of non-existent things are distinct from one another by an essential distinction even in the state of non-existence, so the previous doubt does not apply to them. It may be said that the attribute of sight returns to the attribute of knowledge, and its objects of attachment (ta'alluqat) are different, so it is possible that His knowledge, exalted is He, has a particular attachment to the existent that has been annihilated, different from its attachment to the newly begun existent in its state of non-existence. By this the distinction is achieved and the arbitrariness is removed. It is also said, according to the doctrine of the philosophers (al-hukama', the sages), that the form of the earlier non-existent is inscribed in the faculties imprinted upon the celestial spheres (al-aflak), on the basis that they hold that the forms of all corporeal events are imprinted in them. So it has a particular imaginal form, preserved in its personal unity after its passing away. By contrast, the newly begun existent has no such form before its existence; rather, it has only the universal forms in the higher and lower minds (al-adhhan al-'aliya wa al-safila). When that particular form is brought into being, it is a resurrection (ma'ad); and when that universal form is brought into being, it is a newly begun existent. The philosophically inclined Muslim (al-Islami al-mutafalsif) may claim, in His words, exalted is He, ﴿And with Us is a Book that preserves﴾, an allusion to this. Al-Jalal al-Dawani has a discussion on this matter which is not free from scrutiny in the view of the discerning. Moreover, according to most scholars, resurrection does not depend on the validity of restoring the non-existent, because they hold only that the parts of the dead are scattered, not that they are completely annihilated. Perhaps His words, exalted is He, relating the words of its deniers, ﴿When we have died and become dust, [will we be restored?]﴾, are an allusion to this.

Al-Bukhari, Muslim, Abu Dawud and al-Nasa'i related from Abu Hurayra, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "There is nothing of a human being that does not decay except one bone, and it is the coccyx (ajb al-dhanab); from it the creation will be assembled on the Day of Resurrection."

This is not explicit that all parts other than the coccyx are entirely annihilated, because it is possible that by "decays" is meant that the other parts dissolve into the elements from which they were composed. As for the coccyx, it remains in its boneness, and it is a small part of the bone at the bottom of the spine. From the words of al-Zamakhshari: "The coccyx's matter is a wonder: it is the first thing created and the last thing created."

**Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 50, verse 5:**

﴿Nay, but they have denied the truth when it came to them.﴾ This is a transition (*idrab*) that follows the earlier transition, to show that they have come with something more monstrous than their astonishment, namely denying the truth, which is prophethood established by miracles, at the very first instant and without reflection or contemplation. So it is as if it were a *badal bada'* (a substitution arising from a change of intention) for the first one, and there is no need to posit an elided phrase such as "they did not consider well, but rather they denied," or "the warner did not lie, but they denied."

As for the denial mentioned being more monstrous, it was said: because their denial of prophethood is also a denial of what the prophet announced, which is the resurrection and other things. It was also said: because denying prophethood in itself is more monstrous than denying the resurrection, though this may not hold according to those who hold that reason independently establishes the basic principle of recompense. Moreover, it is possible that they had heard of the resurrection from the adherents of other religions, unlike his prophethood (ﷺ) specifically. It was also said: the intended "truth" is the report of the resurrection. There is no doubt that denial is worse than astonishment and more monstrous, so this is a transition from their astonishment at the warner and what he warned of, to their outright denial. It was also said: the intended "truth" is the Qur'an, and what the transition is directed away from, according to what al-Tibi said, is God's saying: ﴿Qaf. By the glorious Qur'an.﴾ It is treated as a *badal bada'* from the first transition, on the basis that it is a transition away from discourse about the Qur'an and its glory, toward astonishment at the coming of one who warned them of the resurrection that it contains. This is a transition to explicit denial of it, and this entails the denial of everything it contains. Thus it was said, so consider this carefully.

Al-Jahdari read *li-ma* with a kasra on the lam and a light mim. Then the lam is temporal, meaning "at," like in your saying "he wrote it for five days having passed," for example, and *ma* is verbal-masdar, i.e.

"nay, but they denied the truth at the time of its coming to them." ﴿So they are in a confused matter.﴾ *Muḍṭarib*, from *maraja al-khatim fi isba'ihi*, meaning the ring became loose on the finger due to thinness. The attribution is figurative, as in ﴿in a pleasing life﴾, for the sake of hyperbole, by making the confused matter itself the one that is confused, whereas in reality its owner is confused. This consists of their denying prophethood of humans altogether at one time, and their claim that it is suitable only for people of rank and wealth at another time, as indicated by their saying: ﴿Why was this Qur'an not sent down upon a great man from the two cities?﴾ at another time. It also consists of their claim that prophethood is sorcery at one time and soothsaying at another, when they said of the Prophet (ﷺ) at one time that he is a sorcerer and at another that he is a soothsayer. Or it is the variation in their states between astonishment at the resurrection, considering it remote, and denial, and hesitation about it. Or it is their saying about the Qur'an that it is poetry at one time and sorcery at another, and so on.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 50, verse 6:

﴿Have they not looked﴾ i.e., they were heedless, or blind, so they did not look when they disbelieved in the Resurrection ﴿at the sky above them﴾ in such a way that they see it at all times. It has been said: this is evident according to what is commonly known among people, that the thing seen is the sky which is the specific body that will be rolled up on the Day of Resurrection, and it has been described in the verses and the hadiths with what it has been described with. As for what the philosophers (al-Falasifa) hold, that the thing seen is only a sphere of vapour (kurat al-bukhar) or air that appears in this colour, and has no colour in reality, and is below that body, then there is obscurity in it. Some of the eminent scholars said in this context: the apparent meanings of the verses and reports speak of the sky being visible; what the earlier philosophers mentioned, that the celestial spheres are solid, transparent bodies that are not seen, is not accepted at all; likewise, the claim that the seven heavens are the seven celestial spheres is not accepted by the verifying scholars; likewise the existence of a sphere of vapour, and that what lies between the sky and the earth is air of differing parts in subtlety, so that whenever it rises it becomes more subtle, to the point that it may not be suitable for living and does not prevent the blood from coming out through the extremely fine pores for whoever reaches it; and that seeing the atmosphere in this colour does not contradict seeing the sky in reality, even if it is not itself coloured by it, and that would be like seeing the bottom of the sea green from behind its water, and similar things that are seen through an intermediary of one colour while in themselves being of another colour. Indeed, it has been said: seeing the sky together with the existence of the sphere of vapour is like seeing luminous bodies such as the moon and others.

And you know that the scholars adhere to the apparent meanings until a proof appears showing the impossibility of what they indicate, and then they interpret them. And that insisting on reconciling what the Shari'a has stated with what the philosophers have said, while some of it contradicts other parts, is harder than walking on water or ascending to the sky. I say: there is no harm in interpreting an apparent (text) by a near interpretation toward some part of philosophy, if it includes a legal benefit and does not entail a religious harm. I consider fairness to be part of religion, and dismissing a statement out of contempt for its speaker is not befitting of the verifying scholars. This is what has been said. Some have taken "the sky" (al-sama') here to mean the genus of celestial bodies, and that, as you see, is far-fetched. The apparent meaning is that it is the specific body, and that it is the lowest sky (al-sama' al-dunya), i.e., "Have they not looked at the lowest sky ﴿how We built it﴾, made it firm and raised it without pillars ﴿and adorned it﴾ for the beholders with stars arranged in the most wondrous order ﴿and it has no fissures﴾, i.e., no rifts or cracks; what is meant is its being free from every defect and flaw, so this does not contradict the claim that it has gates. Some claimed that what is meant is that its layers are tightly joined together, but this contradicts what has come in the hadith that between every heaven and heaven is a distance of five hundred years; and perhaps the delay of this mention is for the sake of observing the rhyme (fawasil).

It has been said that here it is ﴿Have they not looked﴾ with fa', while in another place it is ﴿Have they not looked﴾ with wa', because the denial of resurrection was mentioned previously, so the follow-up that indicates reasoning toward it was appropriate. The word "looking" (al-nazar) was used rather than "seeing" (al-ru'ya), as in al-Ahqaf, to counter their disbelief in the matter, as if it were said: looking is sufficient for attaining knowledge of the possibility of resurrection, and there is no need for seeing; this is what al-Imam (al-Razi) said. He argued with His saying, glorified is He: ﴿it has no fissures﴾ against the philosophers regarding the impossibility of rupture. You know that negating a thing does not indicate its impossibility, and moreover you have heard the intended meaning of that. The fact that it is not a literal meaning does no harm, due to its being commonly used.

﴿And the earth—We spread it out﴾ means We stretched it out. This does not contradict its being spherical (kurriyya), whether perfectly or imperfectly, with flattening at the two poles (al-qutbayn), because of its great size. ﴿And We cast into it firm mountains﴾ means stable mountains that prevent it from swaying, as the words of God Most High in another verse indicate: ﴿firm mountains lest it sway with you﴾. This clearly indicates that the earth does not move. Some of the earlier philosophers (al-falasifa) disagreed, as do all the philosophers existing today. Some of the Maghribi Muslims (al-maghariba) agreed with them, claiming that the earth moves with the daily motion, along with what it contains of elements, and they refuted the rational proofs of the earlier scholars that it does not move. Would the one who says this disbelieve? That is what is most likely, or not? ﴿And We caused to grow in it every kind of pleasing pair﴾ means every type, ﴿pleasing﴾ means good, which delights and gladdens whoever looks upon it.

Qur'anic quotation: ﴿A insight and a reminder for every servant who turns back (to his Lord).﴾

Here "turns back" (munib) is said to be a metaphor for reflecting upon the marvels of His creation, glorified is He, by treating reflection on created things as equivalent to returning to their Creator. As for "an insight and a reminder," they are two causes (ʿilla, i.e. the reason or purpose) of the preceding actions in meaning, even though they are in the accusative governed by the last verb, or they are governed by an implied verb by way of resumption (istiʾnaf), meaning: We did what We did as an act of giving insight and giving reminder. Abu Hayyan said: they are both in the accusative as verbal nouns (maṣdar, i.e. infinitive of the verb) for an implied verb derived from their own root, meaning: We gave insight and We reminded. The first (view) is preferable.

Zayd ibn ʿAli read (tabṣiratun wa dhikrā) in the nominative, with the meaning: their creation is an insight and a reminder.

And His saying, ﴿And We sent down from the sky blessed water﴾, meaning abundant in benefits. This begins an explanation of how the growing of every beautiful pair, mentioned earlier, takes place. It is coordinated (ʿatf, joining one clause to another by a conjunction) with ﴿We brought forth﴾, and what lies between them, on the last two possibilities, is an interjected clause (iʿtirāḍ, a parenthetical insertion) that confirms what precedes it and draws attention to what follows. ﴿Then We brought forth therewith﴾, meaning with that water, ﴿gardens﴾, many, as the context requires, meaning trees bearing fruit, ﴿and the grain of the harvest﴾, meaning the seed of crops that are meant to be harvested, such as wheat, barley and the like. The construct (iḍāfa, the genitive construction) here links them because of the association between them. The word ﴿al-ḥaṣīd﴾ (the harvested) means "the reaped," an adjective describing an implied noun, as we have pointed out, so it is not of the type of "masjid al-jāmiʿ" (the congregational mosque, a noun-adjective construction), nor is it a metaphor of the first kind, as has been wrongly supposed. The specific mention of the growing of its seed is because it is the primary intended object.

**Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on Surah 50, verse 10:**

﴿And the palm trees﴾ is coordinated (*'atf*) with ﴿gardens﴾. *Nakhl* (palm trees) is an *ism jins* (collective noun), which may be treated as feminine or masculine and may take a plural. It is singled out for mention although it is included among the gardens, to show its superiority over the other trees. The placing of *habb* (grain) between them emphasizes that the palm and the grain are each independent and distinct from the rest, and it also observes the rhyme of the *fawasil* (verse endings). ﴿Towering (*basiqat*)﴾ means tall, or bearing fruit, from *absaqat al-shatu* ("the ewe became pregnant" when she conceived). On this reading, the word is from *af'ala* and its active participle is *fa'il*. The regular form would be *mufil*, so this is one of the rare forms, like *tawa'ih* and *lawaqih* and others of their kind, such as *shadhdhah*, *yafi'* (from *ayfa'a*) and *baqil* (from *abqala*). Its accusative case indicates that it is a *hal* (circumstantial qualifier) in the sense of a *hal muqaddarah* (a future or prospective state).

Qutbah ibn Malik narrated from the Prophet (ﷺ) that he recited *(basiqat)* with a *sad* (*basiqat*, with ṣ), and this is a dialect of the Banu al-Anbar, who replace *sin* with *sad* when it is adjacent to, or separated by one or two letters from, a *kha'* (kh), *'ayn* ('), *ta'* (ṭ) or *qaf* (q). ﴿It has clustered spathes﴾: *nadid* means arranged one above another. The intended meaning is either the piling up of the spathes or the abundance of fruit matter within them. The sentence is a *hal* of the palm trees, parallel to *basiqat*, by way of *taradduf* (synonymous parallel), or a *hal* of the pronoun in *basiqat*, by way of *tadakhkhul* (embedding). It has also been permitted that the *hal* is the prepositional phrase (*lahā*), with *tal'* (spathe) raised as the subject of it.

And His saying, ﴿as provision for the servants﴾: that is, so that He may provide for them. It is a causal clause (ʿillah, cause) for His saying ﴿so We caused to grow﴾. Stating this cause after the first "We caused to grow," which was explained by "to give insight and admonition," draws attention to the fact that the servant's benefit from this should first and most importantly be in terms of remembrance and insight, and only afterward in terms of enjoying it as provision. It is also permissible that ﴿provision﴾ (rizqan) be a verbal noun (maṣdar) derived from the meaning of ﴿caused to grow﴾, because growing is a provision, so it is like "I sat, sitting." And it is permissible that it be a circumstantial qualifier (ḥāl), meaning "provided for." ﴿And We gave life thereby﴾: that is, by that water, ﴿a dead land﴾: a barren land with no growth in it, by making it such that it swelled or produced plants. The masculine form of "dead" (maytan) is because "land" (baldah) means "country" or "place." Abu Jaʿfar and Khalid read "dead" (mayyitan) with a doubled letter. ﴿Thus is the coming forth﴾: a clause in which the predicate is placed first for the purpose of restriction (qaṣr, exclusive emphasis). "That" refers to the life derived from the giving of life. The sense of distance in it indicates the distance of rank: that is, like that wondrous life is your life through resurrection from the graves, not like something contrary to it. In expressing the bringing forth of plants from the earth by "giving life," and the giving of life to the dead by "coming forth," there is an exaltation of the matter of plant growth, a making light of the matter of resurrection, and a establishing of the likeness between the bringing forth of plants and the giving of life to the dead, to clarify the method of analogy (qiyās) and bring it closer to people's understanding. It is also permissible that the kaf (the particle "like") be in the position of nominative, as the subject (mubtada', "the coming forth" being the predicate (khabar). It is reported from al-Zamakhshari that he said: "Thus" is the predicate, and this is the apparent meaning. As for its being the subject, there is one possibility, which is to say: "That coming forth" is a subject and predicate, like "Abu Yusuf, Abu Hanifa," and the kaf takes the place of "like" in your saying "like Zayd, your brother." And it is not hidden that this is a strained interpretation.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 50, verses 12–13:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿The people of Noah denied before them﴾ to the end of the verse is a resumptive clause (isti'naf) brought to establish the truth of the Resurrection (al-ba'th) by showing that all the Messengers, upon them be prayers and peace, agreed on it, and by showing the denial of those who reject it. In this there is also consolation for the Prophet (ﷺ) and a warning to the disbelievers. ﴿And the People of the Rass﴾: it is the well (bi'r) that was never built up. It was also said that it is a valley (wadi), and its people — it was said they were among those to whom Shu'ayb, peace be upon him, was sent. It was also said that they were the people of Handhalah ibn Safwan. (﴿And Thamud, and 'Ad, and Pharaoh﴾) is meant as him and his people, so that it accords with what precedes and what follows. This is like calling a tribe "Tamim," for example, by the name of its father. ﴿And the brothers of Lut﴾: it was said that they were among his in-laws, peace be upon him. So the intended meaning is not true brotherhood by lineage.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 50, verse 14:

﴿And the companions of the Thicket﴾. It is said: they were a people to whom Shu'ayb (peace be upon him) was sent, other than the people of Madyan. They used to dwell in a thicket (aykah), which is a lush, verdant place, and they were named after it. ﴿And the people of Tubba'﴾ (the Himyarite). He was a believer, and his people were disbelievers; for this reason he was not blamed, while his people were blamed. The full discussion regarding what pertains to this verse has already been given in (the commentary on surahs) al-Hijr, al-Dukhan and al-Furqan.

﴿Each one denied the messengers﴾, i.e., regarding what they were sent with of the laws, among which is the resurrection, upon which they all agreed without exception. That is, each people of the mentioned peoples denied their messenger; or each of these denied all of their messengers. The pronoun is singular in consideration of the word "kull" (each) or of each one of them, who denied all the messengers, since they agreed on calling to monotheism and warning of the resurrection and the gathering. Thus denying one of them is denying all of them. The intended universality is for amplification, as in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿and she was given of everything﴾. Otherwise, those among the people of Noah who believed, and likewise others, did believe. Then, what has been mentioned is evident on the assumption that Tubba' was a messenger. Then, on the assumption that he was not, which is what most hold, the meaning of his people denying the messengers (peace be upon them) is their denying those messengers who came before them, who were agreed upon monotheism and the resurrection, and to this Tubba' used to call them.

﴿So My threat became due﴾, i.e., My warning became binding and descended upon them, and it is the word of punishment.

**Page 178**

﴿Have We then been wearied by the first creation?﴾ This is a resumptive clause that confirms the truth of the resurrection, whose denial by the destroyed nations has been related. Al-'ayy (wearying) with respect to a matter means being unable to do it, not being tired. Al-Kisa'i said:

You say *a'yaytu* (I was tired) from fatigue, and *ayiytu* (I was unable) from the cessation of resource and inability with respect to a matter. This is the well-known and more eloquent usage, although many do not distinguish between them. The interrogative *hamza* expresses denial, and the *fa'* conjoins with an implied clause that is indicated by *al-'ayy* in the sense of intending and undertaking. It is as if it were said: Did We intend the first creation, which is origination, and then become unable to do it, so that our inability to repeat it might be suspected? The Imam allowed that the first creation could mean the creation of the heavens and the earth. This is indicated by His saying, glorified is He: ﴿Do they not see that God, who created the heavens and the earth and was not wearied by their creation...﴾. It is supported by His saying, exalted is He, after this: ﴿And We have certainly created man﴾, etc. And that is, as you see, [not convincing].

On the authority of al-Hasan, *al-khalq al-awwal* (the first creation) is Adam, peace be upon him, but this is not the sound view. Ibn Abi 'Ablah, al-Walid ibn Muslim, al-Qursi on the authority of Abu Ja'far, al-Simsar on the authority of Shayba, and Abu Bahr on the authority of Nafi' recited *afa'ayyana* with a shaddah on the *ya'*. It is explained as following the dialect of those who assimilate the *ya'* into the *ya'* in the past tense, saying *'ayya* from *'aya*, and *hayya* from *haya*. When it is assimilated, they attach the first-person plural pronoun of self-magnification, and they do not unassimilate, saying *'ayyana*. This is a dialect of some of the tribe of Bakr ibn Wa'il, as in *raddtu* and *raddana* (becoming *radtu* and *radna*, with the same assimilation), so they do not unassimilate. In this dialect the doubled *ya'* is fatha-vowelled. Had *nا* been an accusative object pronoun, all Arabs would have assimilated, as in *radanā Zayd* (Zayd returned us).

﴿Rather, they are in doubt about a new creation.﴾ This is a conjunction with an implied clause indicated by what precedes it. It is as if it were said: They acknowledge the first creation and do not deny Our power over it, so there is no basis for their denial of the second. Rather, they are in confusion and doubt about a creation that is new. The creation was indefinite and described as *jadid* (new) rather than saying "the second creation," as an indication of the locus of their doubt and their unusual aversion, by His saying, glorified is He: (*jadid*), and that it is a great creation that must be given serious attention, so it has a tidings, i.e., a tidings. The magnification does not refer to the creation as such, so that it could be said that it is less than the first creation. Rather, it refers to what relates to the matter of the responsible person and what he encounters after it. Some of the verifiers said: it was indefinite because, in their view, it was a great matter given their aversion to it. It was also allowed that the indefiniteness is for vagueness, indicating that it was created in a manner that people do not know. The Shaykh al-Akbar, may God sanctify his secret, cited this verse in the context of proving the renewal of substances, like the renewal that al-Ash'ari claims for accidents. Each of them, according to the Shaykh, does not persist for two moments. It is understood from his words, may God sanctify his secret, that this is based on the doctrine of unity, and that He, glorified is He, is every day in a matter. By my life, the verse is far removed from what he says.

And We have certainly created man, and We know what his soul whispers to him. That is, what it speaks to him about, which is what occurs to the mind. Al-waswasah (whispering) is a faint, hidden sound, and from it comes the jingling of ornaments (waswas al-huli). The pronoun in *bihi* refers to *ma*, which is a relative pronoun, and the *ba'* is extra (silah). The verb is *tuwaswisu* (it whispers). It has been permitted that the *ba'* be for accompaniment (mulabasah) or be extra, but this is not the correct view. It is also permitted that *ma* be a verbal-noun (masdariyyah) and the pronoun refer to *al-insan* (man), with the *ba'* making the verb transitive, in the sense that the soul makes man the one in whom the whispering is established. Thus the one who speaks (al-muhaddath) is man, because whispering is like speech, and so it is the equivalent of *haddatha nafsahu bi-kadha* (he spoke to himself about such-and-such). The Arabs say this just as they say *haddathat-hu nafsuhu bi-kadha* (his soul spoke to him about such-and-such). Labid said:

*And the most deceitful of souls, when you speak to it, is that the truthfulness of the soul diminishes hope.*

﴿And We are nearer to him than the jugular vein﴾. That is, We know him and his states; nothing of his hidden thoughts is concealed from Us. This is on the basis that the cause is mentioned and the effect is intended, because nearness to a thing is customarily the cause of knowledge of it and of its states. Or the statement is of the nature of a figurative expression (tamthil). There is no room to interpret it as physical nearness, since He, glorified is He, is exalted above that. The speech of the people of unity (ahl al-wahdah, the proponents of the doctrine of the oneness of being) is among what is difficult to understand for those who do not share their states. *Habl al-warid* (the jugular vein) is an idiom for extreme nearness, like their saying *maq'ad al-qabilah* (the midwife's seat) and *ma'qid al-izar* (the knot of the waist-wrap). Dhu al-Rummah said, as cited in the *Kashshaf*: "And death is nearer to me than the jugular vein." The *habl* is well known, and what is meant here is the vein, because of its resemblance to a rope, and its attribution to *al-warid* (the vein) is for specification, as with *shajar al-arak* (the tree of the arak). Or it is an attribution of the general to the specific, as in other cases, such as *lujayn al-ma'* (the silver of the water). If the *habl* is kept in its literal sense, then its attribution is like that. *Al-warid* is a large vein in the neck. It is reported from al-Atham that it is the river of the body. It is called *al-warid* in the neck, *al-watin* in the heart, *al-abhar* in the back, *al-akhal* in the forearm and thigh, *al-nasa* (the sciatic), and *al-aslam* in the little finger.

The well-known view is that on each side of the neck there is a vein called *warid*. In the *Kashshaf* it is said: "The two *warids* are two veins flanking both sides of the neck at its front, connected to the *watin*; they flow, as seen, from the head to it." So *warid* is on the pattern *fa'il* in the sense of the active participle (fa'il), though it has been said it is in the sense of the passive participle (maf'ul), because the animal spirit flows (yaridu) to it. This is indicated by the statement of al-Raghib: "The *warid* is a vein connected to the liver and the heart, and in it are the channels of the spirit." He said regarding the verse: "That is, We are nearer to him than his spirit." This has also been related from some of them.

﴿When the two receivers receive﴾: they are the two angels assigned to every person, who record his deeds. Al-talaqqi means receiving by memorization, and al-kataba means writing down. "When" (idh) has been said to be an adverb (zarf) governed by "nearer" (aqrab), and the elative (ism al-tafdil, the comparative form) can govern adverbs, since the sense of the verb suffices for them even though it does not govern other things as subject or direct object. The meaning is: He, glory be to Him, knows the state of the human being better than any who is nearer, at the time when the two receivers, the two guardians, receive what he utters. This implies that He, exalted and majestic, is independent of the recording of the two angels, for He, exalted is His station, knows more than they do and is aware of what is hidden from them. Yet wisdom requires it, namely the writing of the two angels, their guarding, and the presentation of their pages on the day when "the witnesses will stand." The servant's knowledge of this, along with his knowledge that God encompasses his deeds, is an increase in gentleness that restrains him from evil deeds and inclines him toward good ones. It has also been permitted that "when" (idh) be a causal particle explaining the nearness. In this view, there is a remoteness in explaining His nearness, in its knowledge sense, by the awareness of the recording guardians. Some scholars preferred that it be a direct object of an implied verb, "remember," so that the nearness remains in its general sense, and because the elative is weak in governing. Although there is no barrier to its governing an adverb, the discourse is intended to establish His power and the comprehensiveness of His knowledge, glory be to Him and exalted. So reflect.

﴿One on the right and one on the left, seated﴾: that is, one is seated on the right and one is seated on the left. The first is elided because the second indicates it. Among its examples is the poet's saying:

He threw at me a matter from which I and my father were innocent,
and out of hunger he threw at me.

Al-Mubarrad said: the original sense is "on the right, seated, and on the left," and then "seated" was moved from its place. The word "qa'id" here is an intensive form (fa'il) in the sense of the participle (mufa'il), like jalis in the sense of mujalis (companion), and nadim in the sense of munadim (boon companion). Al-Farra' held that qa'id denotes the dual and the plural, and that here the dual is intended, so there is no elision, no fronting, and no postponement. It has been objected that the form fa'il is used for both singular and plural when it means "maf'ul" (passive), but here it means "fa'il" (active), and it is valid for that only by analogy to fa'il in the sense of maf'ul.

Scholars differed in determining the place where the two sit. It was said: they are on the molars (al-nājidhīn). Abu Nu'aym and al-Daylami narrated from Mu'adh ibn Jabal, traced to the Prophet (ﷺ): "God was gentle with the two guarding angels, until He seated them upon the molars, and made his tongue their pen and his saliva their ink."

It was also said: on the shoulders. It was said: at the edges of the jaw near the lower lip hair. In al-Bahr (of Abu Hayyan) it is stated that they differed about this and that nothing valid is reported on it. I say also: nothing more has been established to me than what God has informed of, that they are seated on the right and on the left. Likewise, the report about their pen and their ink is not established. I say, as al-Laqqani said after he inclined to the view that the writing is literal: the knowledge of that is entrusted to God, exalted and majestic. I say: the apparent meaning is that they are on his right and on his left in all his states.

Ibn al-Mundhir and others narrated from Ibn 'Abbas that he said: If he sits, one of them is on his right and the other on his left; if he walks, one is in front of him and the other behind him; if he sleeps, one is at his head and the other at his feet.

[p. 180]

﴿Not a word does he utter﴾: he does not throw from his mouth anything, whether good or bad. Muhammad ibn Abi Ma'dan read ﴿yalfazu﴾ with a fatha on the fa'. ﴿But there is with him a watcher﴾: an angel who watches his speech and records it. If it is good, he is the companion on the right (ṣāḥib al-yamīn); if it is bad, he is the companion on the left (ṣāḥib al-shimāl). ﴿Ready﴾: prepared and equipped to write what he has been commanded to write, whether good or bad. The mention of speech specifically is to establish the ruling for action by way of the textual indication (dalālat al-naṣṣ).

There is disagreement about what the two record. Imam Malik and a group said: they record everything, even the groaning during illness. In the commentary of al-Qanani on al-Jawhara (Sharḥ al-Jawhara lil-Qānī), among the matters that must be believed: Allah the Exalted has angels who record the deeds of the servants, whether good, bad, or otherwise, whether speech, action, or belief, whether an intention or a resolve or an affirmation. He, glory be to Him, chose them for this, and they neglect nothing of their duty, whether it was done deliberately and intentionally, or through forgetfulness and oblivion, which proceeds from them in health or in sickness, as the scholars of transmission and narration have related. End of quotation.

In some reports there is an indication that inner speech (al-kalām al-nafsī) is not recorded. Al-Bayhaqi related in Shu'ab al-Iman from Hudhayfa ibn al-Yaman that speech has seven locks; when it comes out through them it is recorded, and if it does not come out it is not recorded: the heart, the throat (al-lahā), the tongue, the two jaws (al-ḥanakān), and the two lips.

Some scholars held that one of the two does not record what is permissible (al-mubāḥ), because it carries no reward or punishment, and recording is for recompense. Thus it would be excluded as a ruling from the general scope of the verse. This was narrated from Ikrimah.

Ibn Abi Shaybah, Ibn al-Mundhir, al-Hakim (who declared it sound), and Ibn Mardawayh related through his chain from Ibn Abbas that he said: "Only good and bad are recorded. Not recorded: 'O boy, saddle the horse,' and 'O boy, give me water.'" Others said: everything that proceeds from the servant is recorded, even permissible acts. When the deeds of his day are presented, the permissible acts are erased from them, and what carries reward or punishment is recorded a second time. This is the meaning of His saying: ﴿Allah erases what He wills and establishes﴾. Al-Suyuti indicated this in some of his treatises, and he proposed as a way of reconciling the two views the position that permissible acts are recorded and the position that they are not.

Something similar was narrated from Ibn Abbas: Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim related from him that he said concerning the verse: everything he speaks of good or bad is recorded, to the extent that his saying "I ate, I drank, I went, I came, I saw" is recorded. Then, when Thursday comes, his speech and action are presented; what is good or bad in it is confirmed, and the rest is cast aside. This is His saying: ﴿Allah erases what He wills and establishes﴾.

Then, according to the view that permissible acts are recorded, the companion of the left records them, as indicated by what Ibn Abi Shaybah and al-Bayhaqi in Shu'ab al-Iman related through al-Awza'i from Hassan ibn Atiyya: a man was riding a donkey and it stumbled with him, and he said, "Ruined!" The companion of the right said, "It is not a good deed, so record it." The companion of the left said, "It is not an evil deed, so record it." Then a call came to the companion of the left: "Record what the companion of the right has left."

It has also come in some reports that the companion of the right is trustworthy over the companion of the left.

This was related by al-Tabarani, Ibn Mardawayh, and al-Bayhaqi in Shu'ab al-Iman from the hadith of Abu Umamah, traced to the Prophet (ﷺ), and in it: "When the servant does a good deed, it is recorded for him as ten like it. When he does an evil deed and the companion of the left wants to record it, the companion of the right says: 'Hold back.' So he holds back for six or seven hours. If he seeks Allah's forgiveness for it, nothing of it is recorded against him; and if he does not seek Allah's forgiveness, one evil deed is recorded against him."

Like seeking forgiveness, as stated explicitly, is an act of obedience that expiates, according to another hadith, in which the companion of the right says: "Leave him for seven hours; perhaps he will glorify Allah or seek forgiveness."

The apparent meaning of the verse is that the ruling is general, including the disbeliever. So with him too are two angels who record what is for him and against him of his deeds. Several scholars have stated this explicitly, and they mentioned that what is for him consists of acts of obedience that do not depend on intention, such as charity and maintaining family ties, while what is against him is much, especially on the view that he is obligated to the branches of the Shari'ah.

In al-Qanani's commentary on al-Jawhara: the correct view is that the good deeds of a child are recorded, while a madman has no guardians (ḥafaẓa) over him, because his condition is not directed toward obligation, unlike the child. The apparent meaning of the verse includes him in the ruling. Al-Jazuli hesitated concerning jinn and angels: whether they have guardians or not. Then he affirmed that the jinn have guardians, and he followed this with the same view concerning the angels, peace be upon them. Al-Laqqani, after quoting him, said: "I have not found this concerning the jinn in anyone else," and it is understood from this that he found it concerning the angels in someone else. Perhaps this is what has been related from some that the intended meaning of "the Spirit" in His saying ﴿The angels and the Spirit descend﴾ is the guardians over the angels. But asserting that concerning them and concerning the jinn requires a transmitted report.

As for the objection to this view concerning angels, that it leads to an infinite regress (tasalsul), it is answered by what is clear to the one who reflects. Then some scholars inferred, concerning the two angels who are with a person, that they are two angels individually, not as a species: for each person there are two who accompany him until his death. They stand at his grave, glorifying Allah the Exalted, praising Him, and proclaiming His greatness, and they record the reward of that for their companion if he was a believer.

[p. 181]

Abu al-Shaykh in al-'Azamah and al-Bayhaqi in Shu'ab al-Iman related from Anas that the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "Allah the Exalted has entrusted to His believing servant two angels who record his deeds. When he dies, the two angels who were entrusted with him say: 'He has died, so permit us to ascend to the heaven.' Allah the Exalted says: 'My heaven is filled with My angels who glorify Me.' They say: 'Shall we remain on the earth?' Allah the Exalted says: 'My earth is filled with My creation who glorify Me.' They say: 'Then where?' He says: 'Stand at the grave of My servant, glorify Me, praise Me, and proclaim My greatness, and record that for My servant until the Day of Resurrection.'" It has also come that they curse him until the Day of Resurrection if he was a disbeliever.

Al-Hasan said: the guardians are four, two by day and two by night. This allows for the possibility of change, namely that each day and night there are four other than the four of the day and night before them, and it allows for the absence of change.

Some said: the angel of good deeds changes, as an honouring of the one who obeys, while the angel of evil deeds does not change, as a concealment for the disobedient in general. The apparent view is that they do not leave the person, although they said that they leave him during intercourse and when entering the place of relieving oneself. This does not prevent their recording what proceeds from him in that state. For them there is a sign of a good deed and of an evil deed, whether these are bodily or of the heart.

Some reports apparently indicate that what is in the soul is not recorded.

Ibn al-Mubarak and Ibn Abi al-Dunya in al-Ikhlas and Abu al-Shaykh in al-'Azamah related from Damrah ibn Habib, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "The angels ascend with the deed of a servant from among the servants of Allah the Exalted, and they multiply it and purify it, until they reach with it wherever Allah the Exalted wills of His dominion. Then Allah the Exalted reveals to them: 'You are guardians over the deed of My servant, and I am a watcher over what is in his soul. This servant of Mine did not sincerely intend his deed for Me, so place it in Sijjin.'" He said: "And the angels ascend with the deed of a servant from among the servants of Allah the Exalted, and they consider it little and belittle it, until they reach with it wherever Allah the Exalted wills of His dominion. The Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on Surah 50, verse 21:

Abu Muslim said: the driver is a devil who was with the person in the world, and this is a weak saying. Abu Hayyan said: the apparent meaning is that ﴿driver and witness﴾ are nouns of genus; so the driver is angels appointed for that, and the witness is the guardians and everyone who bears witness. And ﴿with it﴾ is an attribute of (soul) or (every), and what follows it is its agent because it depends on it; or ﴿with it﴾ is a predicate placed first and what follows it is the subject, and the clause is in the position of an attribute. It was preferred that it be a resumed clause (isti'naf bayani), because the statements after knowledge of them are descriptions, and the content of this clause is not known, so it would not be an attribute unless one claims knowledge of it. And you know that what has been mentioned is not accepted.

Al-Zamakhshari said: the position of ﴿with it a driver﴾ is the accusative as a circumstantial clause (hal) from (every), because it is definite through its annexation to what is in the status of the definite; for the original form of (kull) is that it be annexed to a plural, like the comparative form (af'al al-tafdil); so it is as if it were said: "every of the souls," meaning that this is its original form, and it has departed from it in usage to distinguish between the singular distributive (kull) and the collective (kull). It is not hidden that what he mentioned is an artificial construction which the rules of Arabic do not support. And Talhah read (ma'han sa'iqun), with the ha' emphasized, assimilating the 'ayn into the ha', so both became ha', as they say: "dhahaba mahamm," meaning "ma'hum" (with them).

**Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 50, verse 22:**

As for His saying, Exalted is He, ﴿You were certainly heedless of this﴾, it is related (*mahkiy*) with an implied verb of speech (*bi-idmar qawl*), and the clause is a resumptive new sentence (*istinaf*) built upon a question that arose from what precedes it, as if it were said: "What will be after the Trumpet blast and the coming of every soul with it a driver and a witness?" So it is said: it will be said to the heedless disbeliever when he beholds the realities that he did not affirm in the world, such as the Resurrection and other things, "You were certainly heedless of this which you are now beholding." The address is to the disbeliever, as Ibn Abbas and Salih ibn Kaysan said. The indefiniteness of *ghaflah* (heedlessness), and making him to be in it while it is in him, indicates that it is complete heedlessness, and such is the heedlessness of the disbelievers regarding the Hereafter and what is in it.

It was also said: the clause is related with an implied verb of speech, and it is an attribute (*sifah*) of *nafs* (soul) or a circumstantial clause (*hal*), and the address is general, meaning: it is said to every soul, or it has been said to it, "You were certainly..." The intended meaning of *ghaflah* here is forgetfulness in general, whether it occurs after knowledge or not, and there is no one except that he has some heedlessness of the Hereafter and what is in it. It is also permitted for the resumptive sentence to be on the general address.

Al-Jahdari read (﴿لَقَدْ كُنْتِ﴾) with a kasra on the *ta'* (*kunti*), addressing the soul, which is feminine, and its masculine form in the line "O soul, you are indeed delighted with pleasures" (*ya nafsu innaka bil-ladhdhat masrur*) is according to interpreting it as the person. It is not necessary in the reading of the majority, because the expression with *nafs* in the reported speech does not require taking it into account in what is reported, as is not hidden.

﴿So We removed from you your covering﴾. The *ghita'* (covering) is the veil that covers the matters of the Return, and it is heedlessness, immersion in sensible things, familiarity with them, and restricting one's gaze to them. Calling that a covering is a metaphor, and it is either the covering of the whole body or of the two eyes. On both, His saying, Exalted is He, ﴿So your sight today is sharp﴾ is valid, meaning penetrating, due to the removal of the obstacle to seeing. On the second view this is evident; on the first, the covering of the whole body is also a covering of the two eyes, so removing it from it requires removing it from them.

Some claimed that the address is to the Prophet (ﷺ), and the meaning is: "You were in heedlessness of this which We mentioned, of the matter of the Trumpet, the Resurrection, the coming of every soul with a driver and a witness, and other things. So We removed from you the covering of heedlessness through revelation and the teaching of the Qur'an. ﴿So your sight today is sharp﴾: you see what they do not see and you know what they do not know." But by my life, it is a fallen claim that agrees neither with the context (*sibaq*) nor with the sequence of the discourse (*siyaq*). In al-Bahr, and from Zayd ibn Aslam, there is a statement on this verse whose transmission is forbidden (*yahrum naqluh*), and it is in the book of Ibn Atiyyah, end of quote. Perhaps he meant this, but in the claim that transmitting it is forbidden there is room for discussion.

Al-Jahdari and Talhah ibn Musarrif read with a kasra on all three *kafs* (the *kaf* of *ankin* and what follows it), addressing the soul. The author of al-Lawami' transmitted the kasra on the *kaf* only from Talhah, and said: "I did not find from him the kasra in ﴿You were certainly﴾. If he gave it a kasra there too, then that is that; and if he gave it a fatha, he has treated that in accordance with the wording of (*kullu*, "every"), and the kasra in what follows it in accordance with its meaning, since it is added to (*nafs*, "soul"). This is like His saying, Exalted is He, ﴿So his reward is with his Lord﴾ and His saying after it, ﴿and no fear shall be upon them﴾." End of quote.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 50, verse 23:

﴿And his companion will say﴾

﴿This is what is with me, ready﴾: a reference to the disbelieving person himself, meaning: this is what is with me and in my possession, ready for Hell, which I have prepared for it through my misleading and leading astray. The ﴿mā﴾ is an indefinite qualified by the adverbial phrase and by ﴿ʿatīd﴾, or a relative pronoun whose relative clause is the adverbial phrase. The word ﴿ʿatīd﴾ is a second predicate after the predicate of the demonstrative, or the predicate of an omitted subject. It was permitted that it be a substitute (badal) for ﴿mā﴾, on the basis that it is permissible to substitute an indefinite noun for a definite noun even without being qualified, when the benefit is achieved by the substitution. As for its estimation as "a thing ready" (shay'un ʿatīd), on the basis that the substitute is the omitted qualified noun whose attribute has taken its place, or that the relative ﴿mā﴾, because of its vagueness, resembles an indefinite and so it may be substituted by it, it has been objected that the first is weak because it necessitates omitting the substitute, which the grammarians reject, and the second is not held by those who require the adjective; so it is a settlement without the agreement of the two parties. ʿAbd Allah read ﴿ʿatīdan﴾ with the accusative, as a circumstantial accusative (ḥāl).

﴿Cast into Hell every stubborn disbeliever.﴾ This is an address from Allah, exalted is He, to the driver and the witness, on the basis that they are two and not one comprehensive entity combining both attributes; or it is addressed to the two angels from the guardians of the Fire; or it is addressed to one, on the basis that the alif is a substitute for the energetic nun (nun al-tawkid), with the connecting pause treated as a stop (ijra' al-wasl majra al-waqf). ﴿Withholding from good﴾: exaggerating in withholding wealth from its obligatory rights. Qatadah, Mujahid and Ikrimah said: it means zakah. This has been deemed weak, because if that were the intended meaning, the apparent wording would have been "withholding from good" (with "from" governing "good"). In al-Bahr, it is said: the better view is that "good" is general, covering wealth and other things.

﴿Transgressor﴾: wrongdoing, overstepping the truth and going beyond it. ﴿Doubting﴾: one who is in doubt about God Most High and His religion. It was also said: about the Resurrection.

﴿Who set up with Allah another god﴾ is a subject (*mubtada'*, the topic of a nominal sentence) that contains the meaning of a conditional (*shart*), and its predicate is ﴿cast him into the severe punishment﴾. This is with an interpretation (*ta'wil*) whereby it is said concerning him: "cast him." Or, because it has the sense of the response of the conditional (*jawab al-shart*), it needs no interpretation. Or it is a substitute (*badal*) for (*kulla kaffar*, "every disbeliever") or for (*kaffar*, "disbeliever").

God's words ﴿cast him﴾ are a repetition for emphasis (*takrir li-l-ta'kid*). It is therefore like ﴿so do not think them﴾ after His words ﴿Do not think that those who rejoice﴾. The *fa'* here serves to indicate that the casting is for the described attributes mentioned, or it is of the type of (*wa-haqqika thumma haqqika*, "by your right, then by your right"). The difference between the emphasizing element, the explaining element and the element being explained descends to the position of a difference between two essences in a rhetorical (*khitabi*) manner, and it does not claim a real difference, because emphasis (*al-ta'kid*) rules that out. The statement of the scholars of the science of meanings (*ahl al-ma'ani*), that between the emphasizing and the emphasized there is a strong connection that prevents coordination (*'atf*), is not absolutely correct, while the grammarians hold a different view. Ibn Malik said in *al-Tashil*: "Separating two sentences in emphasis with (*thumma*, "then") is better than joining them, if confusion is avoided." Some grammarians mentioned that the *fa'* also, and al-Zamakhshari mentioned the *waw* in (Surat al-Jathiyah), and they regarded that as technical emphasis (*al-ta'kid al-istilahi*).

If (*al-'adhab al-shadid*, "the severe punishment") were taken as a kind of the punishment of Hell and of its terrors, then it would be of the type of (*mala'ikatihi wa-Jibril*, "His angels and Gabriel") without repetition, and it would be, as the author of *al-Kashf* said, good.

It is also permitted that it be an object (*maf'ul*) of an implied verb which the ﴿cast him﴾ explains. Ibn 'Atiyyah said: it may be an adjective (*sifah*) of (*kaffar*). Describing it with a definite noun was permitted because it is specified by the attributes mentioned. Abu Hayyan criticized this, saying that it is not permissible to describe an indefinite noun (*nakirah*) with a definite noun (*ma'rifah*), even if it is described with many attributes.

﴿His companion said﴾, that is, the devil assigned to him (al-Shaytan al-muqayyad lahu). This sentence was introduced as a resumptive clause (istinaf, a new sentence that resumes the narration without being grammatically joined to what precedes it), like the other sentences occurring in the narration of the exchange, because it is an answer to an omitted element indicated by His words, exalted is He: ﴿Our Lord, I did not make him transgress﴾. It is built upon a prior statement by which the disbeliever made an excuse, as if he had said: "He made me transgress."
