This differs from the first sentence, which must be conjoined (wajib al-'atf) to what precedes it, to indicate the combining of its two concepts in occurrence, namely the coming of every soul together with the two angels. The statement of his companion, ﴿but he was himself in far error﴾, refers to his being in error from the truth in essence, so I aided him in it through seduction and calling him to it, without compulsion or coercion. Thus it is, as we have previously mentioned, a parallel to ﴿I had no authority over you﴾, etc.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 50, verse 28:

﴿قال﴾ is a resumptive clause (isti'naf) built in answer to a question arising from what precedes it, as if it were said: "So what did Allah, exalted is He, say?" It was answered: He, mighty and majestic, said: ﴿Do not dispute before Me﴾, meaning at the place of reckoning and recompense, since there is no benefit in that. ﴿And I had already sent forth to you the warning﴾ concerning rebellion, in the abode of earning, in My Books and through the tongues of My messengers. So do not hope to be freed from it through what you are engaged in, namely making excuses with false pretexts. The clause is a circumstantial clause (hal) in which there is a reason for the prohibition. The meaning of knowledge is taken into account so that the concomitance required by the circumstantial state is achieved, i.e., do not dispute before Me while knowing that I had already sent forth to you the warning, when I said to Iblis: ﴿I will surely fill Hell with you and with whoever follows you among them﴾, so you followed him, turning away from the truth. The ba' is either superfluous (za'idah) or transitive, on the basis that qaddama means taqaddama, which is intransitive but takes ba' as its complement. It is also permitted that ﴿qaddamtu﴾ governs the words of His, exalted is He:

The passage: "﴿The word is not changed in My presence﴾ etc. And ﴿with the threat﴾ is connected to an omitted element and is a circumstantial phrase (ḥāl) of the object, placed before it, or of the subject, meaning: 'And I have already presented to you this word accompanied by the threat, attached to it, or I have presented it to you as a promise to you. So do not hope that I will change My threat.' The more evident view is that this sentence is a new resumptive statement (isti'nāf). Regarding ﴿in My presence﴾, according to what the Imam said, there are two possibilities. The first is that it is connected to 'the word,' meaning: the word that is with Me is not changed. The second is that it is connected to the verb before it, meaning: change does not occur in My presence. He said: On the first view, there are several interpretations concerning the word that is with Almighty God.

The first of them is His Almighty words: ﴿Cast both﴾. They wanted, by their excuse, that He would change it and say, 'Do not cast,' so He answered them.

Page 187

The second is His Almighty words to Iblis: ﴿I will surely fill﴾ etc. The third is the threat in general. The fourth is the word decreed earlier, on the day He created the servants: 'This one is blessed and this one is wretched.' On the second view, there are also several interpretations of the meaning of the verse. The first: 'It is not denied in My presence, for I am All-Knowing; I know who transgressed and who made others transgress. So your saying, "Our Lord, it was Satan who made us transgress," is of no benefit, and neither is the saying of Satan: ﴿Our Lord, I did not make him rebellious﴾.' The second: 'Had you wished that I not say, ﴿so cast him﴾, you would have exchanged disbelief for faith before standing before Me. But now, ﴿the word is not changed in My presence.﴾' The third: 'The word of disbelief is not changed into faith in My presence, for faith at the time of despair is not accepted. So your saying, "Our Lord and our God," will not benefit you. Whoever has uttered the word of disbelief, his saying, "Our Lord, we did not associate partners," and his saying, "Our Lord, we have believed," will not benefit him.'

The well-known view is that 'in My presence' is connected to the verb, with the meaning of 'the word' including both the promise and the threat.

Some who held that the threat and the promise cannot be non-fulfilled in any way have used this verse as evidence. Those who held that pardon for some of the sinners is permissible answered that such pardon is not a change, for the indications of pardon specify the threat. Some of the verifiers said: The intended meaning is the negation that anyone could bring about a change in His presence, that is, in His knowledge, Glory be to Him, or that the word He knows, Mighty and Majestic, be changed. For what is with Him, blessed and exalted, is what is in the reality of the matter, and that does not accept change at all. Most threats are conditioned by the condition of His will, as generosity requires, even if it is not mentioned, as intimidation requires. Thus, whenever pardon occurs because He did not will punishment, there is no change of what is in the reality of the matter. So reflect on this, for it is subtle. ﴿And I am not unjust to the servants﴾ comes to establish the truth in the most emphatic way, and it contains an indication that the punishment of those among the servants who are punished is only on the basis of desert in the reality of the matter. The full discussion of this sentence has already been presented, so recall it.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 50, verse 30:

﴿On the Day We say to Hell, "Are you filled?" and it says, "Is there any more?"﴾ Meaning: mention, or warn, of the Day, etc. Then "a Day" is an object of a implied verb. It has also been said that it is an adverb of time governed by "zallam" (wronging). Al-Zamakhshari said: It may be governed by "nufikha" (it will be blown). As if it were said: "And the Horn will be blown on a Day..." On this basis, "that" refers to "the Day We say," because pointing to what comes after is permissible, especially when its rank is to be placed first. So it is as if it were said: "That Day," i.e., the Day of the saying, is the Day of the threat. It does not need an elision, as has passed in the view in which the reference is to the blowing.

This view, as al-Kashshaf says, has a remoteness, because of its distance from the governing word and the intervention of what is unsuitable as a parenthetical clause, and because the time of the blowing is not the Day of the saying except on the assumption that it is extended, with that event occurring in one part of it and this in another part; and all of this is contrary to the apparent sense, so how much more so when these are combined.

Abu Hayyan said: It is very remote, since it separates the governing word from what it governs by many clauses, so it does not befit the eloquence and rhetoric of the Noble Qur'an. The apparent sense is to keep the question and answer on their literal reality. Likewise in the similar cases of the Fire complaining, being given permission to breathe twice, and the Fire and the Garden disputing. We are bound to believe the apparent meaning unless some obstacle prevents it, and there is no obstacle here, for power is capable, reason permits it, and the apparent texts require the occurrence of what reason permits. The affairs of the Hereafter should not be measured by the affairs of this world.

Al-Rummani said: The speech is by elision of a noun, i.e., "We say to the guardians of Hell." This is not correct.

Many have said: It is a figure of speech, and the meaning is that it, despite its vastness and the remoteness of its regions, We cast into it from among the jinn and mankind group after group until it is filled and does not accept any increase. The interrogation is then for denial, i.e., there is no addition beyond its being filled. This was related from Ibn Abbas, Mujahid and al-Hasan. Regarding the negation of increase, it is permitted that it be on its apparent sense, or that it be a metaphor or figure for seeking much. It has also been said: The meaning is that it is of such vastness that whoever enters it enters, and yet within it there is space and emptiness, so the interrogation is for affirmation, i.e., within it there is room for more because of its vastness. It is also permitted that this is a figure for the intensity of its anger against the disobedient, as if it were seeking to increase them. The claim that there is space in it was questioned on the ground that it contradicts the explicit words of His, exalted is He: ﴿Surely I shall fill Hell﴾, etc. It was answered that there is no contradiction, for "filling" may mean that no tier of it is free of those who dwell in it, even if there is much space, as one says: "The town is full of its people," though there is no empty house in it, with the buildings and courtyards between them. Or that this is by consideration of two states: there is space at the beginning of entering it, then the devils and the like are driven into it and it fills up. Moreover, more than one hadith indicates that it literally seeks increase, except that one does not know the real nature of what is placed in it until it is filled, since the reports on this are among the ambiguous matters whose apparent meanings are not intended according to the majority.

Ahmad, al-Bukhari, Muslim, al-Tirmidhi, al-Nasa'i and others related from Anas, who said: The Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: "Hell will not cease to have people cast into it while it says, 'Is there any more?', until the Lord of Might places His foot in it, whereupon part of it draws in on part and it says, 'Enough, enough, by Your might and Your generosity.' And the Garden will not cease to have room, until Allah creates for it another creation, and He settles them in the spacious parts of the Garden."

The two Shaykhs and others related from Abu Hurayrah, who said: The Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: "The Garden and the Fire disputed. The Fire said: 'I have been given preference for the arrogant and the tyrants.' The Garden said: 'What is wrong with me? Only the weak of people and their outcasts enter me.' Allah, exalted is He, said to the Garden: 'You are My mercy; I show mercy through you to whom I will of My servants.' And He said to the Fire: 'You are only My punishment; I punish through you whom I will of My servants. Each of you will have its fill. As for the Fire, it will not be filled until He places His foot in it, whereupon it says, "Enough, enough." Then it is filled, and part of it draws in on part, and Allah does not wrong any of His creation. As for the Garden, Allah, exalted is He, creates for it a creation."

The interpreters have explained this. al-Nadr ibn Shumayl said: The "foot" is those disbelievers whom Allah, exalted is He, foreknew would enter the Fire, and "qadam" may mean "that which goes before," as in His saying: ﴿a sure standing (qadam sidq)﴾. The apparent sense of the hadith, on this view, requires the entry of others than the disbelievers before them, which is extremely remote; and perhaps there are reports that contradict it.

Ibn al-Athir said: "Qadamahu" means those whom He has sent forward to it from among the evil of His creation, so they are the "foot" of Allah, exalted is He, for the Fire, just as the Muslims are His "foot" for the Garden. "Qadam" is whatever one has sent forward of good or evil. This, as you see, is far-fetched. What refutes it is what is in the hadith of Ahmad, Abd ibn Humayd and Ibn Mardawayh from Abu Sa'id, traced to the Prophet ﷺ: "Its people will be cast into it, that is, the Fire, and it says, 'Is there any more?' And they are cast into it, and it says, 'Is there any more?' until the Mighty and Majestic comes to it and places His foot upon it, whereupon it draws in and says, 'Enough, enough.'"

They interpreted "foot" (rijl) as "a group," and from this is what is reported of Ayyub, peace be upon him, that he was bathing naked when a swarm of locusts (rijl min jarad) fell upon him. The attribution to His pronoun, exalted is He, makes this remote. It has also been said: placing a foot or a leg upon a thing is a parable for restraint and suppression, as if it were said: the command of Allah, exalted is He, comes to it and holds it back from seeking more.

Close to this is what some of the Sufis held: that "foot" is a figure for the attribute of majesty, as "hand" is a figure for the attribute of beauty. It has also been said: what is meant by this is the calming of its ferocity, as one says of a matter one wishes to nullify: "I placed it beneath my foot" or "beneath my leg." These two views are preferable to what preceded them, and Allah, exalted is He, knows best.

"Al-mazid" is either a mimi verbal noun like "al-mahid," or a passive participle whose weak letter is treated as in "al-mabi'."

al-A'raj, Shayba, Nafi', Abu Bakr, al-Hasan, Abu Raja', Abu Ja'far and al-A'mash read "yawma yaqulu" with the third-person ya' (yaqulu). Abdullah, al-Hasan and al-A'mash also read "yuqal," in the passive voice.

﴿And Paradise will be brought near to the God-fearing﴾. He begins to explain the state of the believers after explaining the state of the disbelievers. This clause is a conjunction (ʿatf) upon *nufikh* (the Trumpet being blown), meaning: it was brought near to the God-fearing (*al-muttaqin*), those who guard themselves against disbelief and sins. ﴿Not far away﴾, i.e., in a place that is not distant, within sight of them, before them. In this there is an emphasis which does not lie in omitting the adverbial noun (*zarf*). *Ghayra baʿidin* (غَيْرَ بَعِيدٍ, "not far") is a qualifier of an adverbial noun governed by *uzlifat* (أُزْلِفَتْ, "was brought near"); the noun was omitted, its qualifier took its place, and it took the accusative case in its stead. For this reason it did not say *ghayra baʿidatin* (غَيْرَ بَعِيدَةٍ, feminine). It is also permitted that it be in the accusative as a verbal noun (*maṣdar*), the original being *wa-uzlifat izlafan ghayra baʿidin* ("and it was brought near, a bringing near not far"). The Imam said: that is, away from Our power. It is also permitted that it be a circumstantial qualifier (*ḥal*) of Paradise, used for emphasis, as when you say: "a mighty one, not humbled," because might (*ʿizzah*) is incompatible with humiliation (*dhull*), and negating the opposite of a thing is an affirmation of its confirmation. In this there is a refutation of the supposition that there is some figurative usage or some admixture of its opposite. He did not say *ghayra baʿidatin* according to this. It was said: this is because Paradise is interpreted as a garden (*bustan*). It was said: because *baʿid* follows the pattern of a verbal noun in which masculine and feminine are equal, like *al-zaʾir* (the roaring) and *al-ṣalīl* (the clanging), so it was treated like them and given their treatment. It was said: because *faʿīl* in the sense of *fāʿil* may behave like *faʿīl* in the sense of *mafʿūl*, so both usages are equal in it.

The Imam has several explanations for the bringing near of Paradise. Among them: the folding up of the distance between it and the God-fearing while each remains in its place and does not move from it, and as an honour to the God-fearing. It was said: "﴿And Paradise was brought near to the God-fearing﴾" rather than "the God-fearing were brought near to Paradise." Among them also: the intended meaning is the bringing near of its attainment and entry into it, not a nearness of place; and in this there is what there is. Among them also: the nearness is in its literal sense, and Allah, Mighty and Majestic, is able to move Paradise from the heaven to the earth, i.e., toward the lower direction, or to the earth known after it is stretched out. As for the statement of some: the meaning is that it is made to appear near them, in the manner of its being made to appear to the Prophet (ﷺ) across the wall of his blessed mosque, a view which contains a Sufi tendency.

[Page 189]

This is the commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 50, verse 32:

﴿This is what you were promised﴾ is a reference to Paradise. The masculine form (al-tadhkir) is used because the one referred to is the named entity (al-musamma), without intending any particular word that indicates it; still less is its masculinity or femininity (al-tadhkir wa al-ta'nith) relevant, since these are rules of the Arabic word (lafz), as in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Then when he saw the sun rising, he said, "This is my Lord"﴾, and His saying, glorified is He: ﴿And when the believers saw the confederates, they said, "This is what Allah and His Messenger promised us"﴾. It is possible that this (masculine form) is for the sake of the report (al-khabar) being masculine. It has also been said that it refers to the reward (al-thawab). It has also been said that it refers to the verbal noun (masdar) of ﴿was brought near﴾, and the sentence, with an implied verb of saying (taqdir qawl), occurs as a circumstantial clause (hal) from "those who are God-conscious" or from "Paradise", and the governing element is "was brought near", meaning: said to them, or said concerning it, "This is what you were promised." Or it is an interjected clause (i'tirad) between the substituted noun (al-mubdal minhu), namely "for those who are God-conscious" (lil-muttaqin), and the substitute (al-badal), namely the prepositional phrase; and this is far-fetched.

The form of the present tense (al-mudari') is to bring the past scene vividly to mind (istihdar al-surah al-madiyah). Ibn Kathir and Abu 'Amr read (yu'adun) with the ya' of the third person (ya' al-ghaybah). According to this reading, the sentence is said to be an interjection or a circumstantial clause from Paradise. Abu Hayyan said: it is an interjection, and the intended meaning "this is the thing that was promised" is what you see, and it is as you see.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿for every oft-returning (awwab)﴾, that is, one who returns often to Allah, exalted is He, is a substitute for "those who are God-conscious", by repeating the preposition, or from (lil-muttaqin), on the basis that the prepositional phrase is a substitute for the prepositional phrase. ﴿Vigilant (hafiz)﴾: he who guards his sins until he turns away from them, as narrated from Ibn 'Abbas and Sa'id ibn Sinan. Close to this is what Sa'id ibn Mansur, Ibn Abi Shaybah and Ibn al-Mundhir transmitted from Yunus ibn Khabbab, who said: Mujahid said to me, "Shall I inform you about the awwab and the hafiz? He is the man who remembers his sin when he is alone, and so he seeks forgiveness from Allah, exalted is He, for it."

'Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn Jarir and Ibn al-Mundhir transmitted from Qatadah, who said: that is, one who guards what Allah, exalted is He, has entrusted to him of His right and His blessing.

Ibn Abi Shaybah and Ibn al-Mundhir transmitted from 'Ubayd ibn 'Umayr, who said: We used to count the awwab and the hafiz as the one who is in a gathering, and when he wished to rise he would say, "O Allah, forgive me for what I committed in this my gathering." It has also been said that he is the one who guards his repentance from being broken, and the form awwab does not contradict this, as is not hidden.

"And His saying, exalted is His majesty: ﴿Whoever feared the Most Merciful unseen and came with a penitent heart﴾ is either a substitute (badal) for the whole of what is substituted, [i.e., for "the God-fearing" (al-muttaqin)], or a second substitute for "the God-fearing," on the basis of the permissibility of multiple substitutions with a single substituted-from noun.

As for the statement of Abu Hayyan: "A substitute is repeated while the substituted-from noun is one; this is not permissible except in the substitute of idda' (badal al-bada'), and its secret is that the substituted-from noun is intended for dropping, so it is not substituted again" — this is not accepted. Ibn al-Hajib permitted it in his Amali, and al-Damamini related it at the beginning of his commentary on al-Khazrajiyya and elaborated on it at length.

As for the claim that the substituted-from noun is "intended for dropping," this is not to be taken literally. Alternatively, it is a substitute from the described noun "awwab," meaning "for every person who is awwab," on the basis of the permissibility of omitting the substituted-from noun. Ibn Hisham permitted this in al-Mughni, especially since its adjective has taken its place, so that it is as if it had not been omitted, nor substituted from "awwab" itself, because "awwab" is an adjective of an omitted noun, as you have heard. So if it were substituted from it, the substitute would take its ruling, and thus be an adjective like it. And "man" (من) is a relative pronoun, and relative pronouns do not take an adjective except "alladhi" according to the more correct view. Some permitted describing with "man" as well, but this is a weak view. Or it is a subject (mubtada') whose predicate is..."

By interpretation, "it is said to them," [﴿Enter it﴾] is in the imperative form (al-inshā'iyya, the mood of command or address), and the plural is used in view of the meaning of "man" (man). His saying, exalted is He, ﴿in the unseen﴾ is connected to an omitted element that is a circumstantial clause (ḥāl) from the subject of ﴿feared﴾, or from its object, or it is a qualifier of its verbal noun. That is, a fear mingled with the unseen, in that he feared His punishment, glorified is He, while He is unseen by him. Or it means He is unseen from the eyes, so no one sees Him. It was also said: the ba' is instrumental (lil-ālah), and what is meant by "the unseen" is the heart, because it is hidden. That is, one who feared the Most Merciful with his heart and not with his limbs, by displaying fear while there is none of it in his heart. But this is not correct.

The mention of the title "the Most Merciful" serves to indicate that they, despite their fear of His punishment, mighty and majestic is He, are hopeful of His mercy, glorified is He, or that their knowledge of the vastness of His mercy, blessed and exalted is He, does not prevent them from fearing Him, majestic is His station. Al-Imam (al-Razi) said: It is possible that the word (the Most Merciful) is a reference to what the fear requires, because the meaning of "the Most Merciful" is the Giver of existence through creation, and "the Most Merciful" (al-Raḥīm) is the Giver of continuance through provision. He, glorified is He, in this world is "the Most Merciful" in that He brought us into existence, and "the Most Merciful" in that He sustained us through provision. So the one from whom existence comes should be the One who is feared, and what preceded is more fitting.

The ba' in His saying, exalted is He, (with a heart) is for accompaniment. It was also allowed that it be for transitivity, meaning he brought a heart turning in repentance. The attribution of "turning in repentance" to the heart, although it is the owner who is described by it, is because the point is his return to God, exalted is He. Al-Imam strangely allowed that the ba' is causal, as if it were said: he came only because of the effects of knowledge in his heart, that there is no returning place except God, exalted is He, so he came because of his heart turning in repentance. This is, as you see, odd. His saying, exalted is He, ﴿in peace﴾ is connected to an omitted element that is a circumstantial clause from the subject of (enter it). The ba' is for accompaniment, and "peace" (al-salām) is either from safety (al-salāma) or from greeting (al-taslīm). That is: enter it while accompanied by safety from punishment and the removal of blessings, or with greeting and salutation from God, exalted is He, and His angels. ﴿That﴾ is a reference to the extended time in which some of what has been mentioned occurred. ﴿is the Day of Eternity﴾, the lasting existence that has no end ever. Or it is a reference to the time of entering, with an implied noun: that is the day of the beginning of eternity and its realization, or the day of the decree of eternity. Or it is a reference to the time of entering, with an implied noun: that is the day of the beginning of eternity and its realization, or the day of the decree of eternity. Or it is a reference to the time of peace, with an implied noun also: that is the day of the announcement of eternity, that is, the announcement of it.

*Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani, "The Spirit of the Meanings") on surah 50, verse 35:*

﴿They shall have whatever they wish﴾ of the various kinds of desires, whatever it may be, ﴿therein﴾. The phrase ﴿therein﴾ is connected to "they wish." It was also said that it is connected to something omitted, functioning as a circumstantial clause (ḥāl) either of the relative pronoun or of its omitted resumptive pronoun in its relative clause. ﴿And with Us is more﴾ refers to what does not occur to their minds and is not included within their wishes, of the lofty honours that "no eye has seen, no ear has heard, and it has not occurred to the heart of any human being." From this is what Ibn Abi Hatim transmitted from Kathir ibn Murrah: that a cloud passes over them and says, "What do you desire?" and it rains upon them whatever they desire, so they do not desire anything except that it rains it down upon them.

Al-Bayhaqi, in *al-Ru'yah* (The Vision), and al-Daylami transmitted from Ali, may Allah ennoble his face, that the Prophet (ﷺ), regarding the words of Allah, ﴿And with Us is more﴾, said: "The Lord, mighty and majestic, will manifest Himself to them."

Ibn al-Mundhir and a group transmitted from Anas that he also said regarding this: "The Lord, blessed and exalted, will manifest Himself to them every Friday." A hadith transmitted by al-Shafi'i in *al-Umm* and others also states: "Friday is called the Day of Increase (yawm al-mazid)." It was also said that al-Mazid refers to pairs of wide-eyed maidens (ḥūr 'īn), upon whom are crowns, the least pearl of which illuminates what lies between the east and the west, and upon each of them are seventy garments, and the one who looks will have his gaze penetrate until he sees the marrow of her shin through all of that. It was also said that it is the multiplication of a good deed tenfold.

[p. 191]

﴿And how many We destroyed before them﴾, meaning many.

We destroyed before your people ﴿of generations﴾, peoples living contemporaneously in one time, ﴿who were greater than them in might﴾, meaning in strength, as it has been said, or in severe seizing in every respect, like ʿĀd and the people of Pharaoh. ﴿So they roamed through the lands﴾, traveled through the earth and wandered in it out of fear of death. So *tanqīb* means travel and covering distance, as al-Rāghib and others mention. They recited the verse of al-Ḥārith ibn Ḥillizah:

They roamed the lands out of fear of death,
and wandered the earth in every direction.

And the verse of Imru' al-Qays:

I have roamed the horizons until
I was content with returning as the only gain.

It is also narrated as "and I have wandered (*ṭawwaftu*)." Al-Ṭasttī narrated from Ibn ʿAbbās that Nāfiʿ ibn al-Azraq asked him about this, and he said: "It means they fled, in the dialect of Yemen," and he recited for him the verse of al-Ḥārith mentioned above, but attributed it to Hudā ibn Zayd. He explained *tanqīb* in the lands as "exercising control over them by ruling them and the like." The term *tanqīb* became common in custom with the meaning of searching into a matter and investigating its conditions. From it is the words of the Exalted: ﴿And We raised from among them twelve chiefs﴾ (*naqīban*). *Tanqīb* by travel and the like, as narrated from Ibn ʿAbbās, is for mere sequence (*ta'qīb*). According to explaining it as exercising control, it is causal, because their control over the lands results from the intensity of their might. In both readings it is a conjunction coordinating with the sense of what precedes it, as if it were said: "Their might intensified, so they roamed." It has also been said that it is, in the same way, causal and coordinated with *ahlaknā* (We destroyed), on the understanding that the meaning is "We began destroying them, so they roamed the lands." ﴿Is there any escape?﴾ is either with an implied verb of saying functioning as a circumstantial clause (*ḥāl*) from the *wāw* of *naqqabū* (they roamed), meaning: saying, "Is there for us any deliverer from God the Exalted, or from death?" Or the *tanqīb* is treated, because it contains the sense of pursuing and searching, as if it were a verb of saying, as has been said. Or it is an independent statement denying that they have any escape, meaning: "Do they have any deliverer from God, Mighty and Majestic, or from death?" It has also been said that the pronoun in *naqqabū* refers to the people of Makkah, meaning: they travelled in their journeys and voyages through the lands of the destroyed generations, so did they see any escape for them, that they should hope for the like for themselves?

This is supported by the reading of Ibn ʿAbbās, Ibn Yaʿmur, Abū al-ʿĀliyah, Naṣr ibn Sayyār, Abū Ḥaywah, al-Aṣmaʿī from Abū ʿAmr, *fa-naqqibū* (imperative form), because the imperative addresses those present at the time of revelation among the disbelievers, namely the people of Makkah and no others. The original principle is the agreement of the two readings. In this reading there is a shift (*iltifāt*) from the third person to the second person. Ibn ʿAbbās also read, and ʿUbayd narrated from Abū ʿAmr, *fa-naqqabū* with a *fatḥah* on the *qāf* and without doubling, and the meaning is as in the doubled form. It was also read with a *kasrah* on the *qāf* and lightly, from *al-naqab* with a vowel, which is when the sole of a camel's hoof is worn thin from much travel. The poet said:

By God, Abū Ḥafṣ ʿUmar swore
that no wear or sore had touched them.

The statement then carries an implied *muḍāf* (noun in construct), meaning: "the feet of them were worn." The wearing of the feet is a well-known metaphor for much travel, so the meaning reduces to: they greatly increased their travel in the lands, or: the soles of their mounts were worn out, and the intended meaning is again much travel. The implied elision may also be avoided by making the attribution metaphorical.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 50, verse 37:

﴿Indeed, in that﴾ — i.e., the destruction, or what has been mentioned in the surah — ﴿is surely a reminder﴾ — a reminder and an admonition — ﴿for whoever has a heart﴾ — i.e., a heart that is aware and perceives realities, for one who does not comprehend or understand is as if he were non-existent. In al-Kashshaf (al-Kashshaf of al-Zamakhshari): ﴿for whoever has﴾ and so on is an illustration (tamthil). ﴿Or gives ear﴾ — i.e., listens to what is recited to him of the revelation — ﴿while he is a witness﴾ — i.e., present, in the sense that it is from shuhud meaning presence (huḍūr), and what is meant by it is one who is attentive, because one who is not attentive is treated as one who is absent; so it is either a metaphor (isti'arah) or a metonymy (majaz mursal), and the first is preferable. It has also been permitted that it be from shahadah (witnessing), as a description of the believer, because he is a witness to the soundness of what was sent down and to its being a revelation from Allah the Exalted, so this prompts him to listen well; or as a description of him from the saying of Allah the Exalted: ﴿that you may be witnesses over mankind﴾, as if it were said: he is among the witnesses, i.e., the believers of this nation. So it is a kinayah (allusion) in both aspects; and it has been permitted, according to the first of these two, that it not be a kinayah, meaning that the intended sense is: he is a witness with certainty, not like the witness of the People of the Book.

And from Qatadah: the meaning is for one who heard the Qur'an from the People of the Book while he is a witness to its truth, because of what he finds in his book concerning its description. The most fitting with the context and the fullest in benefit is taking it from shuhud, and the proper reading is to make ﴿while he is a witness﴾ a circumstantial clause (hal) from the pronoun of the one who gives ear, not a conjunction upon (alqa), as is not hidden from one who has a heart; or [the reading] "or gives ear while he is a witness." The intended meaning is that in what was done to the earlier nations, or in what has been mentioned before them of signs, there is a reminder for either of two groups: one who has a heart that understands from Allah the Mighty and Majestic, and one who has an attentive hearing together with a present mind, i.e., for one who has readiness to accept from the scholar, if he is not a scholar himself. And "or" (aw) is for precluding the absence of either, inasmuch as it is possible that a person be a scholar and also ready to accept from a scholar. Some have mentioned that it is for dividing the one who reminds (al-mutadhakkir) into one who recites and one who listens, or into a scholar and a learner, or into a scholar of complete readiness who needs nothing beyond reflection upon what he has, and a deficient one who needs to learn, so he is reminded when he turns with his whole self and removes all the obstacles entirely; so reflect.

And al-Sulami, Talhah, al-Suddi and Abu al-Barhasam read (aw ulqiya) in the passive voice, ﴿al-sam'u﴾ (the hearing) in the nominative as a substitute for the subject (naib 'an al-fa'il); and the omitted subject is either that which was expressed earlier by the relative pronoun, and on the second [reading] its meaning is: for one who caused another to give ear, and opened his ear, but his mind was not present; or it is himself: he has been made to give ear while he is a witness, attentive, present of mind. So the description, namely shuhud, is the basis of the statement, and it was expressed in the verse in this phrasing only for the sake of emphasis upon his alertness and presence. And on the first [reading] its meaning is: for one who gave his hearing while he was present and attentive. Then, even if another relative pronoun were assumed after "or", the one who has a heart and the one who gives ear could be different, though one person, even if not capable, may be two persons, or may be one person considered under two states: the state of his alertness in himself, and the state of giving ear with presence to one who is alert in himself; because "man" (man) is general, encompassing each and every one individually.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 50, verse 38:

﴿And We certainly created the heavens and the earth and whatever is between them﴾ of kinds of created things, ﴿in six days﴾ whose discussion has already preceded. ﴿And there did not touch Us﴾ and did not befall Us through that, although it is of a kind that powers and capacities cannot bear, ﴿any fatigue﴾ of any weariness. Thus the tanwin (nunation) is for diminishing, and this is as Qatadah said. Others responded to the ignorant Jews who claimed that He, exalted is His majesty, began the creation of the world on Sunday, finished it on Friday, rested on Saturday, and reclined upon the Throne. Glorified is He and exalted above what they say, a great exaltation.

It is reported from al-Dahhak that the verse was revealed when they said that, and it is related that they claim it is mentioned in the Torah. The clause ﴿And there did not touch Us﴾ and so on may be either a circumstantial clause (ḥāl) or a resumptive independent clause (isti'nāf). Al-Sulami, Talhah and Ya'qub read (lughūb) with a fatha on the lam, in the pattern of qabūl and walūq, and it is a verbal noun (maṣdar) that is not regular, unlike the form with a damma on the lam.

**Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 50, verse 39:**

﴿So be patient over what they say﴾, that is, over what the polytheists say about the Resurrection of absurd falsehoods based on denial and disbelief. For He who was able to create the world in that short span without fatigue is able to resurrect them and take vengeance upon them. Or [it means] over what the Jews say of the statement of disbelief and anthropomorphism (tashbih).

The discourse is connected to His saying, Exalted is He, ﴿And We created [the heavens and the earth]﴾, etc., according to both interpretations. In al-Kashshaf [of al-Zamakhshari], it is stated that according to the first interpretation it is connected to the beginning of the surah up to this point, and that this is more appropriate than its connection to ﴿And We created﴾ [verse 38], because the discourse is linked part to part up to this point, as is not hidden from the one seeking guidance.

You know that the closer connection, according to both interpretations, is with what we have mentioned: ﴿And glorify your Lord with His praise﴾, that is, declare Him far above incapacity regarding what is possible, and above the occurrence of failure in His reports, among which is the report of the occurrence of the Resurrection, and above describing Him, Mighty and Majestic is He, with anything that entails anthropomorphism (tashbih). Or declare Him free of every deficiency, and among that is what was mentioned, praising Him for what He has bestowed upon you, such as reaching the truth and other things.

﴿Before the rising of the sun and before its setting﴾: these are the two times of Fajr (dawn) and 'Asr (afternoon), and their merit is well known.

﴿And of the night﴾ is an object (maf'ul) of an omitted verb that is explained by ﴿glorify Him﴾, on the basis of generic unity (al-ittihad al-naw'i), and the conjunction (al-'atf) is for personal difference: that is, "and glorify Him for part of the night, so glorify Him." Or it is an object of the Almighty's words, "(Glorify Him)," with the fa' being a conditional fa' (fa' al-jaza'iyyah). The sense is: "Whatever the case, glorify Him for part of the night." The object is placed first for emphasis on it, and so that it serves as a substitute for the omitted element, and so that the conditional fa' stands in its proper place in the middle. Perhaps the intended "part" here is the pre-dawn time (al-sahar), since its excellence is well known. ﴿And the backs of prostrations﴾ means the times after the prayers (a'qab al-salah). It is the plural of dabr, pronounced with a damma and then a sukun, or of dubur with two dammas.

Ibn 'Abbas, Abu Ja'far, Shaybah, 'Isa, al-A'mash, Talhah, Shibl, and the two Ḥaramis (the readers of Mecca and Medina) read ("idbar") with a kasrah on the hamzah. It is a verbal noun (masdar). You say: "adbarat al-salah idbaran," meaning it ended and was completed. The meaning is "and at the time of the ending of prostration," like their saying: "I will come to you at the disappearance of the star" (khufuq al-najm).

Several scholars held that the intended glorification is the prayer, by way of mentioning a part and meaning the whole, or the necessary for the whole, or the thing that necessitates it. On this view, the prayer "before sunrise" is the Subh (dawn prayer), and the prayer "before sunset" is the 'Asr. This was said by Qatadah, Ibn Zayd, and the majority. Al-Tabarani in al-Awsat and Ibn 'Asakir reported from Jarir ibn 'Abd Allah, traced to the Prophet (ﷺ), that: "And of the night is the prayer of al-'Atamah (the night prayer, i.e., 'Isha), and the backs of prostrations are the voluntary prayers after the obligatory prayers." Ibn Jarir reported it from Ibn Zayd. Ibn 'Abbas said: "The prayer before sunrise is Fajr, and the prayer before sunset is Zuhr and 'Asr. And of the night are the two 'Isha prayers, and the backs of prostrations are the voluntary prayers after the obligatory prayers." In another report from him, it is the witr (the odd-numbered prayer) after 'Isha. In another report from him, and from 'Umar, 'Ali and his son al-Hasan, Abu Hurayrah, may Allah be pleased with them all, and al-Sha'bi, Ibrahim, Mujahid, and al-Awza'i, it is two rak'ahs after Maghrib. Musaddad reported it in his Musnad, and Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Mardawayh reported from 'Ali, may Allah honor his face, traced to the Prophet (ﷺ). Muqatil said: "Two rak'ahs after 'Isha, in the first of which he recites ﴿Say: O you disbelievers﴾ and in the second ﴿Say: He is Allah, One﴾." It was also said: "And of the night" is the prayer of the two 'Isha prayers and the tahajjud (voluntary night prayer). From Mujahid: it is the night prayer (salat al-layl). It admits of generality to include both 'Isha prayers and specificity to tahajjud, and the latter is the more apparent.

﴿And listen﴾ is a command to listen, and the apparent meaning is that listening is literally intended. Its object is omitted; the implied sense is: "listen to what I inform you of concerning the terrors of the Day of Resurrection." This is explained by His words, Exalted is He: ﴿the Day the Caller calls﴾ up to the end of the verse. This method was adopted because of the rhetorical effect of first leaving the matter vague and then explaining it, which conveys the magnitude and grandeur of what is being reported. The word ﴿the Day [yawm]﴾ is in the accusative case, governed by what is indicated by ﴿That is the Day of Coming Forth﴾. That is: the Day the Caller calls, they will come forth from the graves. It has also been said that the object is omitted, its implied sense being "the call of the Caller," and it has been said that its implied sense is "the calling of the disbelievers to woe and perdition." The word ﴿the Day [yawm]﴾ is then an adverb of time (*zarf*) for that omitted element. It has also been said that the verb needs no object, and the meaning is: "Be a listener and do not be heedless." It has been said that the meaning of *istama'* is "wait," and that the address is to every listener. It has been said that the address is to the Messenger (ﷺ), and that ﴿the Day [yawm]﴾ is in the accusative as a direct object of *istama'*, meaning: "wait for the Day the Caller calls, for in it will be made clear the truth of what I have said," just as one says to someone you promise the arrival of a victory: "Listen, such-and-such."

According to some reports, the Caller is Jibril (Gabriel, peace be upon him): Israfil blows into the Trumpent (*al-Sur*, the Trumpet), and Jibril calls: "O decayed bones, torn skins and scattered hair! Indeed Allah commands you to gather for the judgement of the reckoning." Ibn 'Asakir and al-Wasiti, in *Fada'il Bayt al-Maqdis*, reported from Yazid ibn Jabir that Israfil (peace be upon him) blows into the Trumpet and says: "O decayed bones," up to the end. Thus the one meant by the Caller is him (peace be upon him). In *al-Hawashi al-Shihabiyya* it is stated that the first view is the more correct.

﴿from a near place﴾: this is the Rock of Bayt al-Maqdis (Jerusalem), according to what has been narrated from Yazid ibn Jabir, Ka'b, Ibn 'Abbas, Buraydah and Qatadah. According to what is narrated from Ka'b, it is the nearest point of the earth to the heaven, by eighteen miles.

In *al-Kashshaf* it is stated that it is nearer to it by twelve miles, and that it is the centre of the earth. You know that such a matter is not accepted except by revelation. Furthermore, that it is the centre of the earth is something the principles of determining latitudes and longitudes reject. For this reason it has been said that the meaning is: near to those he is calling. It was said: he calls from beneath their feet. It was also said: from the roots of their hair, so that every hair hears: "O decayed bones," etc. Some people said: what is meant by its nearness is that the call comes from it, which is not hidden from anyone, but everyone hears it equally. The call in all of this is in its literal sense. It has also been allowed that the restoration is like the word *kun* (the divine word "Be") at the beginning, according to the well-known view; so it is a figurative expression for bringing the dead back to life by mere will, with no actual call or voice. Furthermore, what we have mentioned, that the Caller is an angel and that he calls with what you have heard, is the transmitted report. It has also been allowed that his call is his saying to the soul: "Return to your Lord; you will certainly enter your place in Paradise or in the Fire," or: "these are for Paradise and these are for the Fire." It has also been allowed that the Caller is Allah, Exalted is He, calling ﴿Assemble those who did wrong and their spouses﴾ or ﴿Throw into Hell every stubborn disbeliever﴾, together with His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Enter it in peace﴾, or ﴿Seize him and shackle him﴾, or ﴿Where are My partners?﴾, or other than that. It has also been allowed that someone other than Him, Exalted is He, and other than the angel, from among the accountable beings, calls: "O Malik, let your Lord decree against us," or ﴿Pour upon us some water or some of what Allah has provided you﴾, or other than that. The reliable view is what has preceded.

﴿The Day they hear the Shout﴾: this is the second blast (al-nafkha al-thaniya). (﴿The Day﴾) is a substitute (badal) for ﴿the Day the caller calls﴾, and so on. The governing element (al-'amil) for both is what is indicated by ﴿That is the Day of Coming Forth﴾, as mentioned earlier. It is also permissible that it be an adverbial of time (zarf) for what is indicated by that, while ﴿the Day the caller calls﴾ is not governed by it but by something else, as has passed. And it is permissible that it be an adverbial of time for ﴿calls﴾. The words of the Exalted, (bi-al-haqq, "with the Truth"), are in the position of a circumstantial accusative (hal) from (al-sayha, "the Shout"), meaning they hear it while it is connected with the Truth, which is the Resurrection. It is also permissible that (al-haqq) means certainty (al-yaqin), and the statement is like "he cried out with certainty," meaning the crying out was produced by him with certainty, not like an echo or other things. It is as if it were said: "the Shout that is realized." It is also permissible that the preposition phrase be connected to (yasma'un, "they hear"), so that the meaning is "they hear with certainty." And it is permissible that the letter ba' is for the oath (al-qasam), and (al-haqq) is God Almighty, meaning "they hear the Shout; I swear by God." This, as you see, is far-fetched.

﴿That﴾, i.e., the Day, ﴿is the Day of Coming Forth﴾ from the graves, and it is one of the names of the Day of Resurrection. It has also been said: the demonstrative refers to the call, and the word was extended in its use as an adverbial, so it was made a predicate of the verbal noun; or the sentence contains an omitted genitive-governing noun (mudaf), meaning: "that call is the call of the Day of Coming Forth," or "the time of that call is the Day of Coming Forth."

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 50, verse 43:

﴿Indeed, it is We who give life and cause death﴾ in this world, without anyone sharing with Us in that. ﴿And to Us is the final return﴾, the return for recompense in the Hereafter, not to anyone other than Us, neither independently nor jointly.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 50, verse 44:

﴿The day the earth splits open from them﴾ is a substitute (badal) following another substitute (badal), and it is possible that it is an adverbial complement (zarf) of "the return" (al-masir), meaning: their return to Us is on that day.

Or it is governed by what is indicated by ﴿That is a gathering﴾, meaning: they will be gathered on the day the earth splits open. Nafi' and Ibn 'Amir read (tashshaqqaq) with a doubled shin, and it was also read (tushaqqaq) with a dammed ta', the imperfect of shaqqat, in the passive voice, and (tanshaqqu), the imperfect of inshaqqat. Zayd ibn 'Ali read (tatashaqqaq) with two ta's. The phrase ﴿swiftly﴾ (sira'an) is a verbal noun (masdar) functioning as a circumstantial accusative (hal) from the pronoun in (minhum), interpreted as ﴿hastening﴾ (musri'in). The governing element is (tashaqqaq). It was also said that the implied sense is "they come out swiftly," so it is a circumstantial element from the waw (of the plural), governed by "they come out." Abu Hayyan related this from al-Hawfi, then said: It is permissible that this implied element governs ﴿the day the earth splits open﴾. Ibn al-Mundhir related from Mujahid that he said regarding the verse: the sky will rain upon them until the earth splits open from them. And it has come: "The first whom the earth splits open for is the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ)." al-Tirmidhi, who graded it sound (hasan), al-Tabarani, and al-Hakim related it, and the wording is his, from Ibn 'Umar, who said: (The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "I am the first whom the earth splits open for, then Abu Bakr and 'Umar, then the people of al-Baqi', and they will be gathered with me. Then I will wait for the people of Makkah." And Ibn 'Umar recited: ﴿The day the earth splits open from them, swiftly﴾.)

﴿That is a gathering﴾: resurrection (ba'th) and assembly (jam'). ﴿For Us it is easy﴾: that is, effortless (hayyin). The fronting of the prepositional phrase (ʿalaynā) serves to restrict ease to Him, Mighty and Majestic, for He, glorified is He, is the All-Knowing, the Able by His very essence, whom no matter distracts from another matter.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 50, verse 45:

﴿We know best what they say﴾ concerning the denial of resurrection, the rejection of the clear signs, and other things in which there is no good. This is a consolation for the Messenger (ﷺ) and a threat to them. ﴿And you are not over them a compeller﴾, meaning: you are not empowered over them, forcing them to faith or doing to them what you wish; you are only a warner. Thus the bāʼ (in bi-jabbārin) is extra (zāʼida) in the predicate, and ﴿over them﴾ is connected to it.

It is understood from the words of some of the eminent scholars that jabbār may be from jabbarahu ʻala al-amr (he compelled him to the matter, meaning he overpowered him to it), in the sense of ajbarahu (he forced him), and not from ajbarahu, since the pattern fiʻāl in the sense of mafʻil from afʻala has come only in rare cases, such as dirāk and sirāʻ. ʻAli ibn ʻIsa said: this is not heard except in dirāk.

It is also said: jabbār is from jabara in the sense of ajbara, the dialect of Kinana, and ʻalayhim (over them) is connected to an omitted element which occupies the position of a state (ḥāl), meaning: you are not a compeller who forces them to faith, being a ruler over them. This admits of the sense of implication (taḍmīn) and its absence, so do not be heedless. It is also said: what is intended is forbearance toward them and leaving off harshness toward them. On this basis it was said: the verse is abrogated (mansūkha). It was also said: it is abrogated in another respect as well, by the verse of the sword. ﴿So remind by the Qur'an whoever fears My warning﴾, for others do not benefit from it. Ibn Jarir reported from Ibn ʻAbbas, who said: "They said: O Messenger of Allah, if only you would warn us, then the verse was revealed: ﴿So remind by the Qur'an whoever fears My warning﴾."

How fitting is this conclusion with the opening of His words, glorified is He: ﴿Qaf. By the glorious Qur'an﴾. Al-Shaykh al-Akbar, may his secret be sanctified, has a discourse on His words, exalted is He: ﴿Nay, but they are in doubt about a new creation﴾, and some of the Sufis have a discourse on His words, glorified is He: ﴿And We are nearer to him than the jugular vein﴾, which we pointed to earlier. Some of them take Qaf as an indication of the true Existence which encompasses all existent things, and "Allah encompasses them from behind" (cf. 85:20). It is also said it indicates the stations of nearness, and other things are said. Some of them applied the rest of the verses of the surah to what is within the souls, and this is known with slight attention by one who has slight familiarity with their speech. And Allah, the Exalted, is the Guide to the straight path.
